maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939

speechtext: On the order for motions:

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. In the Edmonton Bulletin of February 23, 1939, appears the following editorial:
Three provinces block the way.
A national unemployment insurance scheme will be set up at the present session of parliament if the governments of Alberta, Quebec and New Brunswick will agree to a constitutional amendment giving parliament power to establish such a system.
This was stated in definite terms by Hon. Norman Rogers on Tuesday. Parliament was

Questions
only prevented making an all but unanimous declaration of approval of such a scheme by the member for Edmonton East, who talked against the clock until closing time. If his idea was to avoid having to take a stand on the issue, he succeeded for the day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext:
What is the
hon. member reading?

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext:
I understand the hon.
member is rising to a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext:
There is no
question of privilege there.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext: This statement is absolutely untrue. I did not talk until closing time, and I did not try to avoid taking a stand on the issue. I definitely stated my stand while speaking. I wish for the benefit of the Edmonton Bulletin to give the true facts of the case.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext: I think the hon. member has stated his question of privilege.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext:
I should like to show
that it was not I who talked the debate out on that day. I think I should have the right-

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext: I think all hon. members understand the hon. member's question of privilege.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext: I am pointing out that none of the members from the three provinces who are accused by this editorial of blocking the way was able to speak until 9.45 on that evening. I think in fairness those members should have been allowed to speak.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. KENNEDY EDITORIAL IN EDMONTON BULLETIN OF FEBRUARY 23, 1939
speechtext: I think the hon. member should resume his seat. He has stated his question of privilege.

speechtext: I desire to ask the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) whether it is possible for him to take any action with respect to the relief of ex-service men among the transient unemployed for whom food and shelter cannot any longer be provided in Ottawa, and who cannot establish domicile elsewhere.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT
subtopic: RELIEF OF TRANSIENT UNEMPLOYED EX-SERVICE MEN IN OTTAWA
speechtext:
If the persons on behalf of whom the hon. member is making
representation are pensioners, they are entitled to unemployment assistance. If they are unfit and unemployable, they are entitled to war veteran's allowance. speechtext:

maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT-APPLICATION FOR LOANS UNDER PART II
speechtext:
No formal applications for loans have been received under part II of the National Housing Act, 1938. speechtext:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: QUESTIONS

2.	The revised table of precedence for Canada 1923 was approved by His Majesty the King and sent to his excellency the governor general by dispatch of the secretary of state for the colonies of the 3rd December 1923.
3.	Yes. Since 1923 the table has been amended by providing a place for former prime ministers of Canada who have held the office of prime minister for at least one year, and by providing that the Prime Minister of Canada shall be placed immediately after the Governor General.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. E. JOHNSTON (Bow River) moved:
maintopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION, SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT COMPANY
subtopic: FIXING OF PRICE AT NINETY-FIVE CENTS PER BUSHEL FOR NO. 1 NORTHERN
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, this parliament should immediately take such steps as are necessary to insure the farmers of Canada a fixed price of ninety-five cents per bushel for number one northern wheat at their local elevator.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity at this session of parliament of introducing the resolution which appears on the order paper in my name. I am aware that the government intends to bring down legislation with regard to farm insurance, but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not intend to dwell on that point, because I think we are all in agreement that some form of farm insurance should be inaugurated in this country; in fact I think such legislation is long overdue. This resolution, however, deals with an entirely different matter, that of a set price for the producers, and I think it is most opportune that we should consider this question now.
I have before me an extract from the Ottawa Citizen of February 20, 1939. This purports to be an interview with the Minister of Agriculture :
Under the new legislation the government will hope to confine its grain marketings assistance to farmers who find themselves hard pressed economically through no fault of their own and only through emergency conditions.
"The new legislation" Mr. Gardiner said in an interview', "will provide machinery by which the government may come to the assistance of an average farmer who farms with an average degree of efficiency and through no fault of his owrn but due to emergency conditions over which he has no control finds himself in danger of losing his farm."
Emergency conditions might mean drought, grasshoppers or the condition of international wheat markets. The aid will be in the form of acreage bonus which will apply to coarse grains as well as wheat. The general resources of the farmer will be taken into consideration, it was learned.
The acreage bonus w-ill be dependent on the extent of cron failure a farmer suffers. For example, a farmer who has a crop of ten bushels to the acre would not receive as much acreage bonus as one whose crop only returned five bushels an acre.
My resolution does not refer to farm insurance. We all realize that that is necessary, but it is an entirely different question and should be treated by itself. I am dealing with the farm problem from a different angle, namely that of the basic price, or the cost of production for the farmers of Canada.
All hon. members will readily see that party politics have no place in a resolution of this type, which deals with a national prob-

Wheat Policy-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
lem; nor shall I attempt to found my argument on behalf of the Canadian farmer, especially the western farmer, on any false premise, but I shall give facts and figures from which no logical argument may arise.
An erroneous impression has been spread in eastern Canada as regards farming in the west. Occasionally one may see in the papers a statement to the effect that some farmer has had a crop of fifty bushels to the acre, and some easterner may visualize fabulous fortunes being made by western wheat growers. It is true that a small portion of a large field, possibly ten acres, may have yielded fifty bushels per acre, but as a general rule the average is much less.
The Dominion Bureau of Statistics gives the average yield per acre for the last five years in the dominion as follows:

It is reported in a book published by the Alberta government, entitled, A Report on the Rehabilitation of Dry Areas of Alberta and Crop Insurance, 1935 and 1936, prepared by the Hon. W. M. Chant, that the average yield in that province is about ten bushels to the acre. According to the statement issued as of January 26, 1939, by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, the average for the last ten year period was 13-84 bushels per acre, and the production in the three western provinces was as follows: .

Or, for the three western provinces the average yield has been 12-3 bushels per acre. . There are many reasons for such a low yield per acre. When I visited the province of Saskatchewan during the month of June last I saw the most wonderful crops that one could imagine. They should have yielded an average of twenty or thirty bushels, and probably would have, had not grasshoppers and cutworms destroyed the entire crop, leaving those farmers destitute. Had it not been for the direct relief they received, some would have suffered severe hardship. Such losses are common, not only in Saskatchewan, but in Manitoba and Alberta as well. Thousands of dollars are spent every year in attempting to control these pests.
If this were the only obstacle that prevented a crop, the situation would not be so
desperate. During the summer and fall of 1938 there was more hail in the province of Alberta than there had been in any other year subsequent to 1928. Of all the forces of destruction I think there is none so devastating as a hail storm. I saw crops in the district in which I live that were almost ready to cut-in fact, one round with the binder had been made. The next day the hail came and completely destroyed it. In places where the grain had stood three or four feet high, not a solitary straw could be seen, nothing but black dirt. Along the sides of the road, hail lay six or seven inches deep -the entire year's work gone in a few minutes; and, worse still, no feed for the stock, nor was there any money for the family to buy the necessities of life.
Large numbers of acres every year in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are dried out. One must not forget that all financial costs had already been expended on this land and not one cent could be returned.
As reported in Hansard, page 138, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said that-
The average price of wheat in Canada for 1936 crop was $1.22 per bushel, No. 1 northern, Fort William.
Further down on the same page, the minister is reported as having said:
Wheat sold in 1937 in Canada at an average price of about $1.31, No. 1 northern.
Such statements give an entirely wrong picture of the true state of affairs. First of all it must be remembered that little No. 1 northern is raised. The proof of this statement I will give a little later in my address. But just here let me give the statement of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics issued on May 13, 1938, relating to the average prices for the year 1936.
They quote the average price at 0-94. Compare this to $122 as stated by the minister. The 1937 average price was SI as compared to the minister's quotation of $1.31. The average price for 1938 as published by the bureau was 0-59. It should here be borne in mind that this does not include cost of freight.
We are fortunate at this time in being able to record the actual cost to the western farmer of raising a bushel of wheat. There were two provinces carrying on this work, Alberta, and Saskatchewan. While both provinces worked independently, it is remarkable to note how nearly the same their results are. The men in Alberta who conducted the experiment had two thoughts in mind: first, what it actually would cost the farmer to raise a bushel of wheat, and second, whether it was

I have here two tables showing the cost of producing wheat, per acre, by horse equipment and by power equipment. No freight is included in either table. This is the cost for the preparation of the land and does not include hauling to the elevator, or freight cost. Without bothering the house with details I should like to have it placed on Hansard.

The other table using power machinery is a little cheaper. The first crop of wheat after fallow is $9.74, plus $1.25 for seed and 50 cents for
hauling which makes $11.49, making the cost per bushel $1-149. For the second crop of wheat the table shows $8.99, which with the $1.25 for seed and 50 cents for hauling makes a total of $10.74 per acre, or $1-074 per bushel as the cost of production. It should be particularly noted that in neither case was there any profit allowed to the farmer. Surely if there is any industry which is entitled to a fair commission on its investment, it is western farming. It has been the consensus of opinion in this house that all the wheat raised in the west is No. 1 northern, and so it has been assumed that the farmers get the full pegged price of 80 cents, but such is certainly not the case.
On January 26, 1939, I received a book from the bureau of statistics entitled Monthly Review of the Wheat Situation, published by authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). On page 34 the following statement appears:
The 1938 wheat crop in the praire provinces is averaging about a grade higher than in 1937, with No. 2 northern the more common grade this year, compared with No. 3 northern a year ago. The best grading from the 1938 crop has occurred in northern Alberta with No. 1 northern predominating. Winnipeg inspections are concentrating in No. 2 northern and are somewhat better than 1937. The effects of rust damage in Saskatchewan in 1938 are shown in Moose Jaw inspections, which are ranging between No. 2 and No. 3 northern, whereas the small volume of inspections in 1937 was predominantly No. 1 northern. Northern Saskatchewan inspections are about the same as last year, varying between No. 2 and No. 3 northern, while central and northern Alberta inspections are going more into No. 2 northern this year, with No. 3 northern the predominating grade in 1937.
Is there an hon. member in this house who dares say that when it costs over $1.10 to raise a bushel of wheat, that 80 cents a bushel is a fair pegged price? No, not 80 cents; for 20 cents must come off the freight, so the farmer gets only 60 cents per bushel for No. 1 northern, but as wheat is mostly graded No. 2 or No. 3 northern, all he actually gets is about 54 cents, less than half of what it costs him to produce the wheat.
A further analysis has been made of this problem in the province of Saskatchewan, to which I have made reference. This appeared in the Western Producer of June 25, 1939, [DOT] and is based on the university farm revenue study. It deals with eleven types of soil as well as with different localities throughout the province, and they have arrived at a definite conclusion in regard to the cost of

There can now be no doubt in the mind of anyone as to what it costs to raise a bushel of wheat. That fact is proven by the investigation made in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta which shows that the wheat growers have been attempting the impossible in trying to produce below cost. Alberta is the best customer of eastern Canada. Ever since the early settlement of the west began there has been a desire to make that portion of the dominion a better market for eastern manufactured goods. So year by year it became a better market. Whenever a crop failure occurred, a decided shortage of sales for eastern manufactured goods took place. In the industrial cities of Ontario and Quebec the factories closed down and men and women of all ages walked the streets in search of employment. A further indication of the contribution which the province of Alberta has made and is making to Canada, and particularly to the central provinces, will be found in the volume of retail merchandising sales within the province. The volume, for the years 1930 to 1934 inclusive, is estimated by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics as follows:
1930		 $176,537,100
1931		 135,095,000
1932		 115,354,000
1933		 108,431,000
1934		 120,423,000
As the years quoted are those of depression, it is obvious that the volume would be considerably higher in the preceding years when the prices of wheat were higher.
It has been estimated that at least seventy-five per cent of the retail merchandising sales consist of goods manufactured in other provinces, principally in Ontario and Quebec. Alberta is indeed a good customer of the eastern manufacturer. Not only does Alberta, along with Manitoba and Saskatchewan, provide a larger market for the manufacturer in other parts of Canada, but annually a large 
volume of business is done in the prairie provinces by the banks, trust and loan companies and life and fire insurance companies, which for the most part have their principal places of business in other provinces.
Again, one has only to consider the elaborate plants and business organizations located in other provinces for the handling of the annual wheat crop produced in the prairie provinces. The principal grain exchange is located in Winnipeg, but there is also an exchange in Vancouver. Numerous large terminal elevators have been erected at Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Fort William, Port Arthur, Toronto and Montreal, while wheat cargoes constitute a large volume of the tonnage carried annually over the great lakes. So also do the great transcontinental railways carry thousands of bushels of wheat from the west. I have in my hand a table compiled from the preliminary returns of the census of the prairie provinces of 1926 and of preceding censuses which shows definitely that Alberta is the best customer for eastern manufactured tractors, combines, motor trucks and automobiles. In 1921 motor trucks were included with automobiles. This statement is true not only of Alberta, but also equally true of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. It includes motor trucks and automobiles on farms, with tractors and combines, and covers the period from 1921 to 1936. It shows that in the year 1921 the number of tractors sold in Canada was, 47,455, of which 38.485 were sold in the prairie provinces; in 1931, the number sold in all of Canada was 105,360, of which 81,659 were sold to the prairie provinces. As to combines, the total number sold in Canada in 1931 was 8,917, of which 8,897 were sold in the prairie provinces. Of motor trucks, 48,401 were sold in Canada in 1931, of which 21,517 were sold in the prairie provinces.
The automobile industry of eastern Canada made a substantial share of its sales in the three western provinces; for in 1921, out of 157,022 sold in Canada, 133,049, or more than half of the total sales, went to the west. Does not this prove that eastern business is dependent upon the success of the western farmer? Why not treat these agriculturists fairly and thus increase the prosperity of all Canadians?
The next table shows the sales of tractors only in the prairie provinces for the years 1920 to 1936. It shows that 95,113 tractors were sold by eastern firms to the prairie provinces in the period from 1920 to 1936.
What would happen to these eastern manufacturers if the farmers of the west went bankrupt? Is this market worth retaining? It is evident from this table that the sales of tractors has fallen off very considerably

Wheat Policy-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
since 1928. Why has this been so? It must be apparent to all that the reason is a lack of purchasing power in the prairie provinces. The farmer has been going behind year after year through no fault of his own, for he has been raising greater quantities of grain; but because he has been producing at a financial loss. A tabulation of the sales of any other item of farm machinery would show approximately the same results.
From these facts there can be no question that the west not only is an excellent customer of the east but keeps eastern people employed in the industries and is directly responsible for the prosperity that Ontario and Quebec enjoy.
It is urgently essential that a closer cooperation and thorough understanding prevail between these two sections of the dominion to ensure the best results for the country as a whole. I feel that it is most necessary at this time, in order to enable hon. members to have this complete understanding, to make an informative statement respecting the financial status of western farmers.
I have outlined some of the conditions of the west which seriously need the attention of every hon. member of the house, not from a partisan point of view, but from the realization that such conditions must cease if we are ever to have a unified Canada working in the interests of the whole dominion. Industrial and agricultural conditions in western Canada are such that no delay should be permitted. The last five years have been years of decided under-crop production, three years of which have been almost total crop failures, and as a result the financial condition of the farmers is such that it is impossible for them to carry on without some assurance of at least the cost of production.
In the early years of the history of the province the tenure of the land was largely that of ownership. In 1901, out of 9,479 farms, approximately 9,076 were held by owners, while only 211 were held by tenants and 192 by part-owners and part-tenanfs. This situation of ownership has changed greatly since then, as is shown by the table, VI, which is taken from The Case for Alberta, published by the Alberta government in 1938. There is not much use in placing the table on Hansard for the information of hon. members, because apparently some of them are not interested in conditions in the west.
The census of 1931 shows that out of 100,35S farms in the province, 67,562 were held by owners, while 16,208 were held by tenants and 16,588 were held by part-owners and part-tenants. It will be observed that since 1931 there has been a decline in the number of farms held by owners, and a substantial increase in the number of farms held by part-owners and part-tenants.
Thus, it is quite evident that the farmers of the west are speedily becoming land tenants rather than land owners.
In 1931, there were 728,625 farms in Canada valued at $4,053,282,300. Of these farms, 242,850 were reported mortgaged to the amount of 8671,776,850. and the average mortgage was $2,776. In Manitoba the average mortgage was 83,165; in Saskatchewan, S3,141; in Alberta, 83.072; in British Columbia, $2,436. In 1936, the average indebtedness per farm in Manitoba was $2,630; in Saskatchewan, 83,023; in Alberta, $2,804. These figures are given by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, May 13, 1938 Again I say probably it will not be worth while putting this table on Hansard, because perhaps some members might not be interested in knowing just what a great contribution the western part of Canada makes yearly to the eastern part of Canada, nor do they realize how urgent it is that we develop a united Canada instead of having, under the present system, a disorganized Canada.
It is evident that the farmers in the west will never be able to pay off their indebtedness unless they have assured them at least the cost of production for the wheat that they raise. We of western Canada have no desire for special privileges, yet we feel that we should have the same consideration that other industries enjoy in the dominion.
Following the wheat conference which was called by the Bracken government of Manitoba, the Western Producer, in its issue of December 29, 1938, published an article having to do with an address by Professor Hope of the university of Saskatchewan, entitled The Burden of Debt, from which I quote:
Professor Hope, Saskatchewan University, threw a glare on the debt situation in Saskatchewan which must have nearly blinded those in the creditor class. The total shrinkage in cash sales from the farm between 1926 and 1938, he said, was $2,700,000,000; for the three years 1931-33 it was over one billion dollars. The farm debt of Saskatchewan alone is $546,000,000, and with wheat at eighty cents a bushel Fort William, more than one-half of the debtor farmers will have to say "No" to the debt collectors. Professor Hope gave production costs for certain areas in Saskatchewan, showing that eighty cents a bushel at Fort William does not begin adequately to meet the situation in Saskatchewan, and presumably in the other two provinces as well. He said: "On the basis of the facts presented if all the -farmers of western Canada were entirely free of debt, or if they did not pay their debts, it would seem that the present farm prices for grain would probably barely maintain a reasonable level of living. It certainly would not maintain a reasonable level of living and enable them to build up their buildings, machinery, homes and personal effects up to the level prior to 1931.

Wheat Policy-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
"Conservatively, it would probably require with average yields a farm price for wheat of average grade of about ninety cents, with coarse grains in proportion, to maintain a reasonable level of living and service the present debt on western farms. It would require somewhat more than this to restore the farming community to the condition of 1931."
The wheat conference that was recently held in Manitoba produced some interesting statistics in that regard, showing the financial position of the west, and that the west cannot carry on unless a farm insurance scheme is provided and, in addition, the farmers receive at least the cost of production.
Some of the leading public men in this country have definitely taken the stand that the price of farm products should not be protected. The present leader of the Conservative party, the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), stated in an address to the people of Edmonton on October 19 last, as reported in the Calgary Albertan of October 20, 1938:
Doctor Manion restated his belief in a moderate protective tariff. Both industry and workmen needed protection against cheap imports. Farmers, except wheat farmers of the west, deserved protection. Wheat farmers could not be protected.

I know that it is the government's intention to bring down legislation as far as farm insurance is concerned. I believe that the whole house is in agreement with such a policy, but that is an entirely different proposition from assuring the farmer a set price for the things he raises, and should be treated as such. For if you are to limit your assistance to farm insurance, where the people will be on a relief standard, they will not be put in a position to patronize eastern industry or pay their debts. Mr. Speaker, the business of farming, if we can call it such, is in a very precarious condition at the present time. It is not news to this house when I say that farming is the backbone of the country to-day, as it has been for a great number of years. In order to support this statement it is necessary only to go back and look up some figures of production of wheat alone. We find that from 1912 to 1938 inclusive the staggering quantity of 8,495,571,700 bushels of wheat was produced, valued at $7,852,066,800. This amount, which represents just one variety of grain, must have had a very beneficial effect upon the building up of the country, because it was distributed directly or indirectly among all classes in all parts of the dominion.
Farming as a business is entirely different from all other industries. Perhaps this accounts for the present condition of the farming population. The farmers, a very numerous body, have to buy from a comparative few who get together and fix prices to suit themselves, the prices usually being whatever the traffic will bear. When the farmer comes to sell his products he is compelled once more to deal with the few, and finds himself confronted with prices set by those who purchase his goods and who are associated with financial institutions through whose help they work their will.
Farmers as a class do everything possible to pay their debts. I must admit that to-day the farm debt situation is not very sound, but I think it will be agreed that farmers have been going through a very tough time. Until some of these adverse conditions are regulated and eased it will be impossible for the farmers to pay all their debts. I personally know of farmers who have gone to the extent of depriving themselves and their families of several of the necessities of life. Statistics show that in the vast majority of cases farmers are living on a far lower standard than numbers of our people who are on relief in the towns and cities. I am not saying this with the slightest idea of dragging down the standard of living of those on relief, because I know that in most cases these people are not on relief of their own choice; they have been put there by circumstances over which they have no control. But I do believe that the standard of living of the farmer should be raised, and probably this can best be done by increasing the price of the farmers' produce and bringing down the cost of the things they have to buy. To the farmer it does not matter greatly whether the price of grain is high or low, so long as the price of the things he has to buy is in proportion.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) has given a very extensive survey of costs of production in Saskatchewan and Alberta. I do not think the figures can be successfully challenged. The Department of Agriculture in a bulletin issued in 1932 gave the average cost of growing wheat as ninety-five cents a bushel. That is basis No. 1 northern at the local elevator. As has been pointed out by a previous speaker, that is much more than the actual amount the farmer gets at the local elevator, nearly twenty cents a bushel being deducted for freight and handling; and where the grade is lower than No. 1 northern, as is very often the
Wheat Policy-Mr. Fair-

case on account of frost, hail, drought, rust and other causes, he is compelled to take a further reduction.
I quote from an address recently given by Major Strange, director of the research department of the Searle Grain Company of Winnipeg:
I have averaged up the price of all wheat produced for sixty-two years and I find it comes out to $1.14 for No. 2 northern at "Winnipeg. I suggest that this is a very good average price.
No farmer would find the slightest fault with this price. The trouble is however that in some years great fluctuations have occurred. For instance it went as high as nearly $3 a bushel in 1918 and as low as 38cents a bushel in December, 1932.
There is another item which I believe has been lost sight of, whether intentionally or not, by most of those who have given figures on cost of production; I refer to interest. Knowing from experience that the interest on a farmer's debt runs to about twenty-five cents on every bushel of wheat he grows, this should be taken into consideration when considering the cost of growing wheat. A number of economists have figured out the cost of interest, their estimates running in some cases as high as thirty cents a bushel, but I believe from information we can secure that twenty-five cents for every bushel grown is a reasonable figure. The debt situation is one which must not be lost sight of, and as just one way of relieving this I suggest a reduction in the interest on Canadian Farm Loan Board loans. A reduction of two per cent could be effected without doing any one any material damage, and would help to a great extent the borrowers from that board.
In Winnipeg from December 12 to December 15 last there was a conference on markets, and Professor Hope of the university of Saskatchewan had this to say:
A few years ago a member of the Department of Farm Management of the University of Saskatchewan made a careful analysis of 195 farm loans in the prairie area. These loans were placed from 1910 to 1927, but most of them from 1920 to 1925. By 1933, 41 were paid off, 36 were foreclosed and 84 were still current. The average debt against current loans was $9.87 per acre compared with an original loan of $11.79 per, acre, after an average duration of twelve years. The interest rate was 8 per cent. Based on the twelve years of payment history of current loans from 1922 to 1933, these farmers were able to pay about 3 per cent annually on the appraised value of the farm real estate. As the total farm capital includes live stock and machinery as well as real estate, it appears reasonable to infer that on the average they could not earn more than 3 per cent on their total capital investment payments in good years.

The best lands had a better payment history than the figures quoted and the poorer lands much worse. The results of this study indicated that either the poorer lands were appraised by the loaning company at too high a figure, or else the amount loaned was too great.
A study of the loaning operations of one of the largest loaning agencies in Saskatchewan is now being undertaken. Preliminary results of this investigation also indicate that on the average the farmer borrowers have earned about 3 per cent annually on the appraised value of the real estate alone, which is not all the farm capital.
In his conclusions Professor Hope said:
On the basis of the facts presented, if all the farmers of western Canada were entirely free of debt, or if they did not pay their debts, it would seem that the present farm prices for grain, would probably barely maintain a reasonable level of living. They certainly would not maintain a reasonable level of living and enable them to build up their buildings, machinery, homes and personal effects to the level prior to 1931.
Conservatively it would probably require with average yields a farm price for wheat of average grade of about 90 cents, with coarse grains in proportion, to maintain a reasonable level of living and service the present debt on western farms. It would require somewhat more than this to restore the farming community to the condition of 1931.
In the light of the present world wheat situation a further drastic debt reduction policy is a partial solution of the western farm problem.
It has been suggested that farmers should learn how to live on a lower standard in order to meet the present debt situation. But any policy that compels such a solution does not solve the problem if we hope to maintain our present social system.
If we consider the basis on which farmers do their business, and compare it with the basis on which government operations are carried on, I think it is clear that the farmer is carrying on his operations in a better way and more economically than governments and some other lines of business. It is suggested that farmers cut down the cost of production to meet the requirements of the market, but it is impossible to put this suggestion into practice, because once land is broken it is not desirable to let it go into disuse. If it is not worked, it will grow weeds, and we all know the damage caused by crops of weeds. If prices and demand are not satisfactory to the manufacturer, he can close his factory and save a lot of the overhead. Speaking of overhead, it was also stated at the Winnipeg conference that fixed charges run anywhere from fifty to seventy per cent of the cost of production of wheat. This shows that the greater the degree of control of production of the various commodities the greater the resistance to a decline in prices. In the free market system and under complete competition decreased demand is translated into decreased prices. In the system of control decreased demand is translated into decreased production. So we see the two extremes; the agricultural implement industry, with great control, drops production eighty per cent and encounters a reduction of six per cent in prices, while the farmers encounter a drop of sixty-three per cent in prices for farm products when their production is decreased only six per cent.
Taking 1929 as the basis, statistics gathered by the League of Nations show the following comparative declines in production and prices as of 1932: In the United States the decline in production was 46-2 per cent and the decline in price 29 per cent. In Canada the decline in production was 41-9 per cent and the decline in price 27 per cent. In Germany the decline in production was 46-7 per cent and the decline in price 28 per cent. In the United Kingdom the decline in production was 16-5 per cent and the decline in price 7 per cent. In the same period agricultural production maintained an increase of 3 per cent and agricultural prices declined as much as 58 per cent in Canada, 57 per cent in the United States and 49 per cent in the Argentine, while in European countries where governments intervened to shelter their farmers the decline was less, averaging about 35 per cent in Germany, 37 per cent in Italy and 28 per cent in Great Britain.
The opinion has been, and I believe still is, held by some hon. members that the price of wheat in western Canada is of interest to the west only. I would point out that the prosperity of all Canada depends a great deal on the price of our wheat in the west. This 71492-85
fact is recognized by Major H. G. Strange, of the Searle Grain Company, who in a recent broadcast said:
This is a most serious matter that every one of us in the west and many in eastern Canada should consider.
The entire economic structure of western Canada; the railways with all their branches; primary and high schools; our roads, both country, market and gravel; our municipalities; our vast elevator system for handling grain; our hamlets, villages, towns and cities; our governments; our universities, have all been built up and populated with over two million people in the expectation that the west would be able to keep in production the amount of acreage it now has in wheat, about twenty-four million acres, which on an average would produce around four hundred million bushels a year, and which would make it necessary to export to some ninety-two different countries between 250 and 300 million bushels a year. As production declines from these levels, so unquestionably will the population of the west decline; so unquestionably will the cost of everything the farmers buy and the cost of selling all their produce increase. So, therefore, will tens of thousands of workers be thrown out of employment, including a number of the farmers themselves. So will the standard of living of everyone on the land, in towns and cities, decline. It is a sad and distressing picture for the future, unless the situation can be remedied. These words, I believe, present the picture as far as other parts of Canada are concerned, because, though merchants and others do not wish to admit the fact, their prosperity depends entirely on the prosperity of the farmers.
Several estimates have been made as to the amount necessary to bring reasonably up to date the equipment of farmers, including tractors, farm machinery, horses, harness, outbuildings as well as their homes and furniture, clothing, and so on; but I believe an estimate of $500,000,000 is reasonable. You will readily understand, Mr. Speaker, that a great many people in Canada would benefit if that amount of money were put into circulation. It would mean that the railroad workers, the manufacturers and labour in general would be benefited. I believe it would also cut down the number of unemployed and reduce the number on relief, thereby removing the necessity for some of the taxes we are paying at the present time.

I think that is enough to show some of the things we are up against. I believe it also shows how difficult it is to regulate prices or acreage or production. This year we may have a crop of twenty or twenty-five bushels to the acre, and next year nothing at all. I believe we have now advanced sufficient argument to convince the house that the farmer is not and has not for some time been receiving his costs of production. Because it is desirable that the farmer should be kept in business, something must be done to guarantee him at least his costs of production, along with a reasonable profit.
The next question is: How shall we deal with this problem? Several suggestions have been made with which I shall not take the time to deal, but I would like to give one or two instances. A sit-down strike was advocated by a meeting of Cooperative Commonwealth Federation farmers at Yegreville. This meeting was addressed by the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Rowe) and Mr. Irvine, a former member of this house. I do not think a sit-down strike will help the situation in any way. What we must do is create more purchasing power and place it in the hands of those who grow our wheat as well as those who are in business across the country.
Another suggestion is that the four great wheat exporting countries of the world should get together. These four countries export eighty-six per cent of the world's total volume of exports, sixteen other countries exporting the remaining fourteen per cent. I think this country should take the lead in getting together with the other exporting countries and doing something about this problem. A suggestion has been made to cut down acreage. That may be all right, and then again it may not be all right. If everyone in the world

was getting enough to eat I believe we should have to produce still more, but as many have not the wherewithal to buy, something must be done.
The least this government can do is to guarantee the farmer his costs of production, and ninety-five cents a bushel for No. 1 northern at the local elevator seems to me to be a reasonable basis on which to work. Up to the end of the 1937 crop year the farmers of Canada had been subsidized to the extent of $12,719,901. As this method of subsidizing seems to be sound for other lines of industry, there is no reason why it should not be sound in the case of the farming industry when such disastrous conditions prevail. A direct subsidy has been paid to or provided for the manufacturers of farm implements by way of tariff protection, and we have paid thousands of dollars annually to the steamship companies. Large amounts of cash and millions of acres of land have been turned over to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Large amounts have also been expended on roads . to give access to mining areas, and tax removals in different forms have been provided for mining companies.
In the past the farmer has paid a large share of the taxes that have been collected to pay these subsidies, and apparently he has a lot of paying to do yet, judging from the increase in our national debt. It is only fair to point out that a large amount of the taxes the farmer pays is paid indirectly, because the whole structure rests squarely on the shoulders of the primary producer. For a number of years the United States has bonused its farmers to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars, as has France, Australia and the Argentine. At the present time farmers in Germany are being paid $2.25 a bushel for wheat; in Italy they are receiving $2.15 a bushel, and in France, $1.50 to $1.60 a bushel. The quality of the wheat in all cases is far below that of Canadian wheat. I believe the farmers of Canada should receive just as good treatment as the farmers of other countries. We are compelled to compete with them on the world market, and it is impossible to do that because we are forced to buy on a protected market, whereas those from whom we purchase are running their prices higher than we are able to bear.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to discuss the problem raised by this motion, although there is a resolution standing on the order paper in my name somewhat similar to the one now under discussion. However, that resolution may never be reached.
At the outset may I say I am not convinced that ninety-five cents a bushel at the local elevator is the price that should be set. That is something that will have to be inquired into very carefully, and I shall have more to say about it a little later.
The resolution which has been presented this afternoon deals with one of the basic conditions of the rehabilitation of western Canada. I should like to say again what I have said before, that the problem of the rehabilitation of agriculture is not directly a western problem. It is a problem which involves the whole Dominion of Canada. Upon the ultimate success of our rehabilitation schemes will depend the economic welfare of the country in which we live.
I do not propose to discuss this afternoon the various newspaper stories which have emanated from this city since the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made his statement a short time ago. I am going to wait until the bills are presented to the house in order that we may have a clear understanding of what it is intended to do in regard to this particular matter. But there are some points which I think should be placed before this house, because I am convinced that many hon. members are not aware of the general condition of the western farmer and the economic situation with which he is faced. Some think that perhaps the provinces should assume more of the burden of their own rehabilitation, but the Saskatchewan brief presented to the Rowell commission clearly indicates that even the normal expenditures of Saskatchewan cannot be met on the basis of taxation now in effect in that province.
In the proceedings of the conference on markets for western farm products, held at Winnipeg in December under the leadership of Premier Bracken of Manitoba, there are to be found data a study of which one can recommend to members on all sides of this house, particularly those from other than western constituencies. For example, a paper was presented at the conference by Professor Hope, and in the discussion which followed it was quite noticeable that Professor Hope's general statements were not in any respect seriously challenged. I propose, therefore, to place before the house some of the conclusions at which Professor Hope arrived.
He showed first the disastrous decline in the value of farm products in recent years. At page 150 of the report of the conference he says:
The Dominion Bureau of Statistics estimated that for the period 1926 to 1929 the average annual cash sales of farm products in the three prairie provinces amounted to about $530,640,000. For the three years 1931 to 1933 the annual average amounted to $164,439,000, a reduction of $366,201,000 per year. For these three years alone, 1931 to 1933, the total reduction in cash income amounts to over one billion dollars compared with a similar period of three years before the depression and drought period. Cumulating each annual deficit below the average 1926 to 1929 figure of $530,000,000, the total shrinkage in cash sales up to 1938 amounts to approximately $2,700,000,000. The debt structure of western farmers prior to 1929 was based on the assumption that this total deficit would be in the form of income in the years following 1929. The unfortunate turn of events since 1929, has resulted in some debt reductions, worn out equipment, depleted homes and clothing and in some cases impaired health of the farm population. And the story is not finished.
Thus Professor Hope paints a word picture of western agriculture. He goes on to say
Wheat Policy-Mr. Coldwell

that these conditions resulted in the intolerable burden which made dominion aid essential. He says:
The Saskatchewan brief before the Rowell commission on interprovincial relations, after exhaustive analysis estimated the total farm debt of Saskatchewan at December, 1937, to be approximately $482,000,000. In 1938 practically no interest was paid on this debt, only half the taxes were collected, direct relief and seed and fodder have been given on a big scale following the widespread drought of 1937. It is estimated that the total debt increased about $64,000,000 during the past year and now stands at $546,000,000 or about $18 per acre of crop land, or about $25 per acre of seeded crop.
Then Professor Hope, at the conference, proceeded to show that this debt situation, originating not only in crop failures and in depression but in low prices, was only a part of the picture. He goes on to say, on the same page:
But the total farm debt is only a part of the story. Ten years in which a combination of prices and yields have reduced two-thirds of the farming population to a subsistence level, and a steadily mounting debt, have left their mark on the physical equipment of the country. The Saskatchewan brief estimated that it would require at least $200,000,000 to bring the farm buildings, machinery, household furnishings and clothes of the farmers of Saskatchewan up to the moderate standards of 1931. Since this figure was calculated another year of partial depletion has been experienced. Under the circumstances the $200,000,000 which amounts to $1,450 per farm is conservative. Over the drought area itself, comprising two-thirds of the province it would be close to $2,000 per farm.
Then he tells other parts of Canada that on a Fort William price of eighty cents for No. 1 northern these obligations cannot be met and western agriculture cannot prosper. He says:
There is a feeling prevalent among some people who are not entirely conversant with the west, that because of the numerous cancellations of indebtedness, such as taxes, relief and arrears of interest, the debt situation is solved and it only needs average yields with present prices to clear up the whole situation. Such is far from the facts. It is true many concessions by creditors have been made. But in Saskatchewan at least, due to a continuance of unfavourable climatic conditions for the past two years and low prices this year, a situation has been reached where considerably more than half the farmers with average yields and present prices for wheat (80 cents basis Fort William) cannot hope to liquidate their debts and restore the conditions of their farms and homes to the predepression level.
I shall not go over all of the ground that Professor Hope covered in relation to the costs of production. This no doubt will be thoroughly discussed when the bills to be presented by the government are brought down, and the question of costs of production can wait until then. But I should like to

point out that allowing living costs, not on as high a scale as the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) suggested a few moments ago, but at from $700 to $850 per year for the average farm family, with average yields, Professor Hope says:
Conservatively, it would probably require with average yields a farm price for wheat of average grade-
Not No. 1 northern, mark you, but average
grade:
-of about ninety cents, with coarse grains in proportion, to maintain a reasonable level of living and service the present debt on western farms. It would require somewhat more than this to restore the farming community to the condition of 1931.
And this ninety-cent farm price estimated by Professor Hope for the average grade is for wheat from average land. The minister pointed out that there are lands that can produce a bushel of wheat for considerably less than ninety cents, but Professor Hope states that, taking the lowest cost of production he quotes for a bushel of wheat in the Regina and Rosetown areas, not one per cent of Saskatchewan farmers have the requisite machinery and the proper type of land to produce wheat at that relatively low cost.

not only the problems of unemployment and industry, but also the problems of the dairy farmer and the fruit grower both in the east and along the Pacific coast. We all know that when there was money in western Canada our people were able to buy eastern products, and the entire country benefited. I should like to emphasize once more that while other branches of industry, like mining, have in the last few years to some extent compensated our general national economy for the loss in the returns from western Canada, yet the day will surely come again when we shall be made to realize from bitter experience that agriculture, and not mining or something dependent perhaps on war industries, is the great basic industry of Canada. So this is a national problem of wide implications.
I was glad to hear the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), who preceded me, make the point that wheat is not the only farm product to be considered. The time is rapidly approaching, in my opinion has already come, when this country will have to adopt minimum prices for various other farm products. At the moment we are discussing grain, so I say that with coarse grains almost worthless in many areas in western Canada, the time has come when we must consider the whole problem of grain and the advisability of adopting fixed minimum prices for coarse grains as well as for wheat. I have on my desk at the moment a telegram which I received yesterday from the directors of the Rosetown cooperative association. The Rose-town district is almost exclusively wheat growing. They urged that if an acreage bonus is to replace a fixed minimum price for wheat, the bonus should apply on all cereal crops, regardless of the size of the farm. But the point I am making is that we must realize that other grains must receive some protection in the price level as well as wheat.
To my mind the price level should be considered entirely apart from the problem of drought and of sub-marginal lands. These latter problems ought to be dealt with by crop insurance and suitable forms of rehabilitation. In the general discussion which is going on in the country at the present time these problems are being confused, but they are distinct and separate. Perhaps the government's bills will help to clarify that situation. I hope that we shall not get them confused here or in the bills which are to be presented, because to my mind they are distinct problems requiring separate treatment. The time has come when the problem of submarginal land will have to be tackled by the authorities, the problem of crop insurance

carefully considered, and the matter of the fixed price considered apart from either of these problems. I do not know to what extent the federal department has inquired into the crop insurance system that has been adopted in the United States, but I understand that Premier Bracken of Manitoba has again given a good lead by sending down a group of legislators to Washington to look into the "ever normal granary" experiments of the United States Secretary of Agriculture.
A low fixed price and an acreage bonus will in my opinion be unsatisfactory. It would tend to keep sub-marginal land in cultivation, and not make for careful cultivation or the maintenance of a high quality product. Hence I say these problems should be considered separately. If, as I said a little earlier, more and more the success of our agriculture is to depend on' quality rather than quantity of the product that we place in the world's markets, in any scheme recognition should be given to the production of a high quality product. Also the adoption of any set minimum price involves orderly marketing. In my view orderly marketing cannot be undertaken in a market half speculative and half controlled. In other words, we must have either one thing or the other, the open market or orderly marketing through a government board. We have tried the speculative market for years and found it unsatisfactory; to-day other countries in the world are setting prices and marketing through government boards, and I believe the time has come when a board or boards representative of producer interests should have the responsibility of marketing all our farm produce.
If there are still those who think the marketing of our products at low prices will win back the lost markets, I do not believe that opinion can be upheld to-day. A flow of cheap ' wheat will not wash down hostile tariff walls and remove the embargoes of the European dictators. We must face the grim reality, regrettable though it be, that self-sufficiencies and nationalisms across the sea have entirely altered the picture as far as marketing our wheat is concerned. Hence it seems to me that instead of looking overseas for a solution, waiting for trade to improve and all that, the problem is right here on our own door step and requires not only our best efforts but the very best brains we can find in the country to do the thing that has to be done. I believe we are more and more being forced to the conclusion that this involves planning of our agricultural production, and

Wheat Policy-Mr. McKenzie (Lambton)
the adoption of minimum prices, crop insurance and a comprehensive national marketing scheme.
I noticed that the hon. member for Battle River spoke of a Cooperative Commonwealth Federation meeting urging a sit-down strike. Of course strange resolutions are often presented at local meetings and carried, but that certainly does not mean that the organization with which I am connected believes in that method of dealing with this problem. In fact we have long been on record. Our Regina manifesto of 1933, and the platform subsequently published, in regard to farming calls for:
(f)	The setting-up of marketing boards for primary products under growers' control.
(g)	A guaranteed minimum price, based upon the average cost of production over an average period of years, to reduce the disparity between the prices of agricultural and industrial products, and to provide the farmer with an adequate standard of living.
In an explanation regarding that issue published by our national office we find these words:
The proposals submitted in this plank are clear, practical and urgently needed. A guaranteed and adequate minimum price must be adopted by the government for farm products. This, together with the abolition of monopolies which exploit the farmer, the adjustment and reduction of accumulated debts, suitable schemes of crop insurance and the development of cooperative organizations and marketing boards enabling the organized farmer to mind his own business, are fundamental requirements of a rehabilitated agricultural industry. Moreover, the problem is national in its scope and effect and must, therefore, find its solution on national and not on provincial lines.
So this afternoon I have endeavoured to place before the house our point of view. I have also placed before the house a few excerpts from a document which I wish every hon. member would read, the proceedings of the conference on markets for western farm products which was arranged by the government of Manitoba and held in Winnipeg from December 13 to December 15, 1938.
It seems to me that if this parliament is going to grapple with this problem, the members of this house must have the picture clearly in their minds. I know there are still some people who think the west, like a poor relation, is dependent upon the east. That is not true. After all, western Canada has, in bygone years, produced vast quantities of new wealth, upon which the great buildings and great industries of eastern Canada were largely founded. So, Mr. Speaker, I have pleasure in supporting the resolution, although I have reservations with regard to the suggested price, which I do not think may be high enough.

Mr. H. A. MeKENZIE (Lambton-Kent): I did not intend to speak on this resolution, Mr. Speaker, and I shall be very brief in my remarks. When I came into the house this afternoon and read this resolution, I thought it was not too bad, that it would take in all Canada; but when I saw that it referred to No. 1 northern, I knew at once it had to do only with the three western provinces. Canada is an agricultural country, and to my mind the problems of the farmers are the most important problems before the people to-day, because at least forty per cent of the people live in rural districts and derive their livelihood from some branch or another of agriculture. I believe that a prosperous agriculture means a prosperous Canada, and further I believe that we shall never be economically sound in this dominion until the producers of primary products receive much better remuneration than they do today.
I have every sympathy for the western farmer; I should like to see him get ninety-five cents or a dollar or even more a bushel for his wheat, but the setting of a minimum price for wheat has proven rather dangerous this year. I assume that step was taken under the wheat board act which, if I remember correctly, was passed in July, 1935, enabling the government to set a minimum price for wheat in the western provinces. Since that time I believe the government have taken some action each year in regard to the price of wheat.
I wonder how the government arrived at the minimum price of 80 cents a bushel for No. 1 northern wheat, basis Fort William, this year. On looking up the market quotations I find that on August 4, when the minimum price was fixed at 80 cents, the Winnipeg market closed at 86$ cents for cash wheat and 76$ cents for October futures. For several weeks futures prices on world markets had been fluctuating moderately, based approximately on the August 4 level, sometimes rising a few cents above it. For example, at Winnipeg on June 1, October futures sold at 76$ cents, and on August 4, at 76$ cents. In the meantime they had fluctuated between a low of 73J cents and a high of 891 cents. On the same dates October futures in Liverpool had been at 82 cents and 83$ cents, and in the interval ranged between 82 cents and 91 cents. September futures in Chicago, on the same dates, sold at 69$ cents and 68$ cents, ranging between 67$ cents and 83$ cents. So probably the government should not be blamed too much for setting the figure at 80 cents, but how did it work out? Well,

1352	COMMONS
Wheat Policy-Mr. McKenzie (Lambton)
as we all know, it has worked out rather badly and is expected to cost the taxpayers of Canada approximately $48,000,000.
But, Mr. Speaker, that $48,000,000 went to the people who had good crops; for last year the wheat crop of the west has been estimated at from 250,000,000 to 300,000,000 bushels, and, as I have said, the benefit of that legislation went to the people who had the crops. It seems to work on the basis of the old parable concerning the talents: To the man who had ten talents were given ten more; to the man who had five talents were given five more, but from the man who had one talent was taken away even that which he had. So the basis was this: To him that hath shall be given, and from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath. That certainly did not help the men on relief at that time; they are still on relief. The man who did not have a crop did not share in that $48,000,000, which went to reimburse western farmers for their bountiful crop. That seems hardly fair to the remainder of the farmers of Canada.
Ontario farmers produce approximately 20,000,000 bushels of wheat a year, and last year they had to sell their wheat at approximately fifty cents a bushel. But they did not get fifty cents, because they had to give up part of that price in order to reimburse the western farmer who had a good crop and who had received more for his wheat than the Ontario farmer was paid.
The western farmers say, " Oh, but have we not paid tribute to Ontario industrialists for many years?" Well, the Ontario farmer has paid the very same tribute, and it must be remembered that the farmers of Ontario outnumber the farmers of any single province of the west. According to the bureau of statistics there are 170,660 farmers in Ontario, 115,000 farmers in Saskatchewan and 85,000 farmers in Alberta. The Ontario farmers live under the same tariff regulations and restrictions that affect the western farmers, and the only possible difference between them is in connection with the freight haul.
I must say that I oppose this resolution asking for a set price of ninety-five cents per bushel. I believe that the wheat board act should be amended or should be removed from the statute books altogether, and that any such legislation should deal with the whole of Canada. Ontario farmers are not at all prosperous. Perhaps we have not as great a wheat problem; but farmers engaged in dairying, poultry raising and other branches of agriculture are not receiving the cost of production for the produce they have to sell.

Again I say I have every sympathy for the western farmers, but this minimum price certainly works out very badly. I am sorry to have to take this stand; but I am not thinking so much about the western farmer, the eastern farmer, the industrialist or any other individual. I am at least trying to think of the people of Canada as a whole and what is in their best interests. This resolution, if adopted, would not give the same advantages to all the farmers of this country, so I must oppose it.

speechtext:
I
had not thought of speaking on this motion, Mr. Speaker, but I believe it is my duty to express my opposition to it. The motion reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, this parliament should immediately take such steps as are necessary to ensure the farmers of Canada a fixed price of ninety-five cents per bushel for number one northern wheat at their local elevator.
In the first place I think the motion is useless, in view of the recent declaration by the Minister 'of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that there would be no more fixed prices for wheat. In the second place, if we are to help the western farmers I think there are other tillers of the soil who are in as great difficulty as the farmers of the west. I have particular reference to the dairy farmers of eastern Canada. If the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), who moved this resolution, is sincerely interested in agriculture, as I believe he is, I think he should have suggested a plan under which all the farmers of Canada would obtain some advantage.
I suggest that the dairy farmers of Canada are entitled to particular help at the present time. During the past few years the federal government has guaranteed a certain price for western wheat. There were good reasons for making such regulations. Western farmers have to face a situation which is anything but satisfactory. They are exposed to soil drifting in the early spring. On some occasions they have to seed their land over again, if they can afford to buy the seed for the second operation. In June and July they are exposed to excessively hot winds which burn the growing wheat grass. They are exposed to hail storms which destroy whatever crop they may happen to have. They are exposed to the dangers of frost and rust which every year do substantial damage in some wheat fields. Finally, when the crop is harvested they cannot always sell it. Indeed, the west is far from being an ideal location for farming.
I am familiar with conditions in the west. I have hundreds of acres of land in Saskatchewan

Wheat Policy-Mr. Brunelle
which, since 1929, have brought me no income. I feel, however, that is my difficulty, and not one which the ratepayers of the whole country should be asked to carry. If I lose money in the west, and if my properties do not pay I do not believe I am justified in asking compensation from anybody else. I should like other farmers in the west to take the same attitude as I take.
There are farmers in Ontario and Quebec, and some in my constituency particularly, who at one time or another have had to sell their butter and cheese at prices which have allowed them no profit whatever. There are legions of farmers in those two provinces who can scarcely make ends meet, simply because they do not obtain reasonable prices for their products. Dairy farmers need assistance, and need it badly. The commodities they must buy are sold at high prices. Farm machinery, despite recent reductions, is being sold at exorbitant prices. In fact, all the necessities of life on the farm must be purchased at prices which necessitate a much higher income. Yet, in spite of their difficulties, the eastern farmers have never had any bonus or special compensation for their losses. They have never been guaranteed any set price. I have submitted on other occasions, and I again say, that particularly the eastern dairy farmers should have assistance. Is it not as expedient to guarantee the eastern farmers a certain price as it is to give that guarantee to others?
I would ask the hon. member for Bow River to pay a visit to some of the eastern farmers. I do not suggest that he should see the farmers who are living in the vicinity of the big cities; let him visit those who live in the remote sections of Ontario and Quebec. If he were to do so, he would find out that the plight of our farmers in the east is not such as will enable them to help others very much longer.	[DOT]
I know the government is unable to pay the deficit of every producer; I know it is impossible to assure success to all, but I repeat that if we are to help one class of farmers we should help the whole class-not a class within a class.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of the principle of the resolution now before the house. What I shall have to say will be both brief and general in nature, because the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has already outlined a wheat policy, the details of which are not yet before the house. I believe it would be unwise in a debate on the resolution to enter into a discussion of those details, and for that reason I shall confine myself to the principle of a guaranteed price for agricultural products.
I should like to say, however, that on the 16th of this month I listened with keen interest to the speech of the Minister of Agriculture in which, very vaguely and indefinitely, he outlined a wheat policy. Very few of us know any of its details, unless we have been following closely the western papers. From day to day I have been deeply interested in noticing articles by Chester Bloom, in which a number of proposals are set out. For instance, I notice Thursday's paper contained the statement, "Production cost of wheat may be set at sixty-three cents", and Saturday's has the following in red ink:
Bigger bonus on smaller yields. Three separate bills to cover Ottawa's new grain marketing policy for dominion.
I do not know whether or not it is becoming a habit with the government, but members of parliament have either to go to banquets or to read the press of two or three hundred miles away to find out what impending legislation is going to be. We shall, however, be glad to see it when it does comes down, and to learn something about the details at that time.
1354	COMMONS
Wheat Policy-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
First of all, may I say a word or two respecting the observations of the two hon. members who have preceded me. Naturally they have expressed the point of view of men representing eastern agriculturists. I have a great deal of sympathy with their point of view. I have spent a good many weekends in the rural districts of Ontario and have seen conditions such as have been outlined by the previous speaker. This last weekend I found I had even more admiration for the Ontario farmer. I went out to a country point, got snow-bound and had to stay there overnight. If the Ontario farmer is able to travel over roads similar to the one I came over this morning, he deserves all my admiration.
I should like to say to the hon. gentlemen that we are not asking that the eastern farmer should do something for the western farmer. What we are trying to do is to point out that the same people who are exploiting the western farmer are also exploiting the eastern farmer, and that the same economy which makes it almost impossible for the western farmer to maintain a decent standard of living is having exactly the same effect upon the eastern farmer. When we ask for a fixed guaranteed price for our agriculturists, we are not asking that for western Canada alone, we are asking it for all farmers generally. Their problems are similar even though their products may be different.
The statement was made by one of the previous speakers that the fixed price for wheat was going to cost in the neighbourhood of $48,000,000. That may be debatable; but leaving it at that, I should like to point out that according to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) we are operating to-day under a fiscal system which takes $86,000,000 from the western farmer in terms of the goods he has to buy, and gives him back only $30,000,000, which leaves a deficit of $56,000,000. As has been pointed out again and again, the wheat producer is perhaps the only agriculturist who gets practically no benefit from the system of protective tariffs which we have in Canada. The hon. member who preceded me said that apart from the long freight haul, the problem of the eastern and the western farmer was the same. That is not so. While the eastern farmer buys his goods in a protected market, he is able to sell in a protected market most of the commodities he produces. The western farmer, particularly the wheat producer, sells almost exclusively on a world competitive market, while he buys in a protected market which raises the cost of the commodities he has to purchase.

I do not want to raise the issue of the east versus the west. I think the plight of the farmers across Canada is serious. When I hear a man like the premier of Ontario saying at a banquet in Toronto last fall that the east is like an old milch cow which the west had been milking for years, all I can say is that if the western farmers have been milking that cow for some years, they have been feeding it for all the years. They have been feeding it in terms of tariff protection, high prices for machinery and the necessities of life, high freight rates, increased cost of implements of production and increased interest rates on the money they have been compelled to borrow.
It is not my intention at this time to deal with this subject at any length, but I should like to touch on one or two phases of the principle of this resolution. First, I should like to deal with the justification for fixing a guaranteed price. I should like to draw to the attention of the house the fact that the farmers are operating with increasing costs and decreasing incomes. Over a period of years, while the prices they have received for their products have been dropping, the cost of producing those commodities has not dropped in proportion. I should like to refer to the proceedings of the conference on markets for western farm products, called to sit in Winnipeg by Premier Bracken. I refer to page 17, which contains a statement by Major Strange, a wheat economist, who is, I believe, connected with the Searle Grain Company. I quote a short paragraph as follows:
However, the cost of production for farmers of western Canada to-day is about 37 per cent more than it was before the war. The greater part of that is owing to the tariffs of Canada, and the other smaller portion of it is due to the higher hourly rates of wages of labour. But the greater portion is from the tariffs.
I direct the attention of the house to that statement.

I am opposed to a tariff that makes it necessary for a man to pay more for what he has to buy unless the government is prepared to give him some compensation for the extra price he is now compelled to pay. I object to the farmer having to buy in a protected market and sell in an unprotected market. If he is to be asked to sell in an unprotected market, he should be allowed to buy in an unprotected market. But the fact is that he is compelled to buy in a protected market, to protect certain eastern interests. I have no objection to setting up an economy that tends to protect industry in eastern Canada; but I say that, in compensation for the benefits received, eastern industry ought to be prepared to see that those

Wheat Policy-Mr. Blackmore
whose costs are thereby increased will receive a square deal by means of compensating adjustments.
I want to point out in conclusion that since we cannot-and I believe it is evident that we cannot-under our existing fiscal system reduce, at least .to any appreciable extent, the cost of agricultural production, we are bound to do for the farmer what we are doing for other industries, namely, guarantee him a cost of production which will be commensurate with a decent standard of living. I have in my hand the bulletin issued by the Searle Grain Company on Thursday, February 16. The author is discussing the very objections to this plan which have been mentioned by some hon. members opposite. He says this:
A dispatch from Ottawa was published also on February 13th to the effect that there seemed to be in Eastern Canada a realization that public finances of the dominion could not stand an annual drain of the present wheat price guarantee of eighty cents, and that the present policy would lead to serious increase in wheat acreage.
The Bracken conference of course must have taken objections of this kind into consideration. We, however, for our own part would like to suggest that these do not appear to be very valid. It has been often shown that eighty cents for No. 1 northern Fort William is still well below the cost of production of wheat by the great bulk of the farmers, and as such, certainly is no inducement for producers to increase their wheat acreage.
May I make just one other citation in support of what I have said? Referring again to Professor Hope-who, I think, with Professor Britnell, is one of the best agricultural economists in western Canada, and one of whose work the people of Saskatchewan are proud-I find the professor has this to say:
On the basis of the facts presented, if all the farmers of western Canada were entirely free of debt, or if they did not pay their debts, it would seem that the present farm prices for grain would probably barely maintain a reasonable level of living. It certainly would not maintain a reasonable level of living and enable them to build up their buildings, machinery, homes and personal effects up to the level prior to 1931.
Conservatively it would probably require with average yields a farm price for wheat of average grade of about ninety cents, with coarse grains in proportion to maintain a reasonable level of living and service the present debt on western farms. It would require somewhat more than this to restore the farming community to the condition of 1931.
So I submit to this house that, while the problem of all farmers demands the attention of this parliament-and like my desk-mate, I agree that we ought to study seriously
the possibility of fixed guaranteed prices for all agricultural producers-the wheat producers of Canada, whether west or east, have a special claim upon our attention because, while their costs of production are held more or less stable by virtue of the economy under which we live, they have continued for the past seven or eight years to sell their products on the Markets of the world at a figure that has not given them a decent standard of living for themselves or enabled them to meet their obligations, and consequently has worked a hardship upon the business people with whom they are associated.
