speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) desires to close the debate.
I should like to have heard a statement from him earlier in the debate on this important question. I do not think any more important question will come before the house this session than that which we have been discussing this afternoon. In view of the statement made a few days ago by the minister, it would have been a splendid thing if we had had a statement from him earlier to-day.
World marketing conditions at the present time are more or less demoralized; the situation in which the producer finds himself is extremely uncertain. This afternoon the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) referred to the report of the conference called by Premier Bracken, which was held in Winnipeg. I followed the proceedings of that conference rather closely, and I have summarized briefly what I think took place, and some of the decisions reached.
They reviewed agriculture, past, present and future. They found that the price trend on many primary products was definitely down. So far as wheat was concerned, the price was only half to-day what it was a year ago. In fact a larger crop this year has resulted in about $30,000,000 less to the producer. Certain questions were considered, and I shall give briefly the answers:
Question 1: Is there a shrinkage in world's
demand?
Answer: Yes.
Question 2: Is the annual production maintained in Canada?
Answer: Yes.	.
Question 3: Is the low price likely to continue?
Answer: Yes.
Question 4: Is the carry-over likely to
increase?
Answer: Quite probable.
The general view of the conference was that the present picture represents world conditions of an extraordinary character.
The present problem to be solved, it was decided, was the control of production, and the question was asked: Can we reduce the cost of production and control the cost of production at the same time?
While there was no definite recommendation made at the conference, we know a committee was set up to carry on further investigation. It was considered, however, that the two main factors in relieving the difficulty would be to find export markets or regain lost markets, and to lower the cost of production. In addition, it was apparent that the prairie provinces have the major responsibility, but it was also apparent that they have no desire to shirk their responsibility.
All this goes to prove that we are in a critical position with respect to marketing.
I have had a little experience in different ways with respect to wheat growing and wheat marketing. As a grain dealer I have operated a private elevator, and I think I can speak with a little authority. I have had some experience on committees of this house dealing with the wheat problem, particularly when Mr. McFarland was here in 1934 reviewing his stabilization operations, when a committee of nine of us reviewed the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and at a later time when Mr. Murray's operations as head of the wheat board were reviewed.
I watched the operations of the board in its handling of the 1938 crop, and at this point I want to say that before the system of having a wheat board and marketing through that board, with a fixed minimum price, is condemned-and I assume there is truth in the statement we have read in the press and those we have heard in the house from the Minister of Agriculture to the effect that the wheat board is to be set aside so far as the handling of wheat is concerned-we should have a thorough investigation into the operations of the board in handling the 1938 crop.
I shall not take time to-night to deal with their operations in detail, but I think it is evident that the policy they pursued had a depressing effect and has resulted in a considerable portion of the loss which the Minister of Agriculture forecast we might have to take. I say that this loss is a direct result of their policy, and a matter which should be investigated thoroughly.
All sorts of evidence can be produced by authorities in the United States and Canada who are closely associated with the grain business. Before proceeding further, I wish to lay before hon. members three or four outstanding facts. This afternoon hon. members to my left had much to say about the condition in which the farmers of the west find themselves. I am going to try to give another picture to-night. I do not think we should parade our difficulties as they seem to want to do from time to time. The farmer
Wheat Policy-Mr. Perley

of western Canada realizes that he has made a contribution to this confederation, and all he wants is fair consideration.
The development of prairie wheat farming was sponsored by the whole of Canada. Wheat farming in western Canada was an important industry long before our mining industry, our textile industry, our paper industry or many of our other industries became real, national assets. But this great national wheat industry is now being threatened by subversion and, therefore, it has become the obligation of the whole of this dominion. The west was encouraged to produce during the war, and production was increased considerably.
There is another fact I should like to call to the attention of hon. members. During the last twenty-eight years the western provinces have produced, according to the bureau of statistics, 9,500,000,000 bushels of wheat. The average yearly production over that period is 340,000,000 bushels, and the average export, around 250,000,000 bushels. The average price for No. 1 northern at Fort William was $1.27, while the average price for all grades was in the neighbourhood of ninety cents. These are figures I think we should keep in mind. In the last twenty-eight years new wealth to the extent of $10,450,000,000 has been produced. What does that mean to industry in eastern Canada? What does it mean in the way of purchasing power, in the way of payments for labour and in many other ways?
In the last three years the production of coarse grains, that is, oats, barley, rye and flax, was valued at $231,000,000, even though these crops were sold at low prices. This afternoon reference was made to the fact that oats had sold at as low as eleven cents a bushel this year. I would direct attention also to the fact that we paid freight averaging about fourteen cents a bushel on that wheat. This amounted to an average of $27,500,000 a year. In the twenty-eight year period, we had paid over one billion dollars in freight, apart from lake freights. I want hon. members to note that this is on wheat alone. I shall not review the amount of money invested in the purchase of machinery, as reference has been made to this already. It is, however, interesting to note that the west purchased $20,000,000 worth of machinery annually. The freight on that machinery during that period amounted to about $250,000,000. All this must have meant something to industry and to the general business of this dominion. I am giving this side of the picture in order to impress upon hon. members the importance of this great industry in western Canada.
I do not propose to go in detail into the plans I suggested. I have a resolution on the [Mr. Periey.l
order paper, but I do not know whether it will be reached. I should like to have had an opportunity of discussing it, but possibly I may be able to say something when the bill comes down. I hope the minister will inform the house to-night when he expects to bring down his bill. The reports which have gone out from this house have more or less excited the whole of Canada, and certainly the west is interested in having this information. Apparently this matter is important enough to have brought provincial authorities and members of the wheat pool here to Ottawa. I understand that these gentlemen are in this city at this time, and I do hope we shall have something definite in a few days.
I believe the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) was in order to-night. When an hon. member proposes to the house a plan or scheme which will need money to carry it out, it is only fair that he should be given an opportunity to show how the money can be obtained. With the scheme I have in mind I believe that over a long term of years the wheat industry could stand on its own feet. That is where our farmers want to be. They do not want to be coming to Ottawa, to eastern Canada, all the time with their hands out. We should have a proper board with proper authority. There should be producer representation on that board, and it should have the courage to act. I believe the advisory board should have been reinstated, with farmer representatives. With such a board I believe the wheat industry could carry on by itself. Later on, I may have an opportunity of outlining what I think can be done. I have definite ideas as to how we can control production and marketing.
From what I have seen announced in the press as to the scheme proposed by the minister, I want to warn him that crop insurance is a different matter from marketing. The two must not be confused. There is another point to consider. I do not think the wheat board can be scuttled for the next year. There certainly will be a large carryover, and any other board or pool which might be set up and financed by the government to carry out a fixed minimum price policy will be in competition with the present board in connection with the surplus which it will have to carry over. That is an important point to keep in mind.
I suggest to the minister that he deal adequately with this question. We want something of a permanent nature. We do not want a board in to-day and out to-morrow. We did not have a board in 1936 when wheat was selling at $1.22, and in 1937 when it was selling at $1.31. They could have paid

Wheat Policy-Mr. Gardiner
the price suggested to-day quite handily and had a nice reserve set up. That would have been the proper thing to do in order to keep this on a business basis. Unless this is done, the minister is going to find himself in a worse position, and the problem will be harder to deal with later on. I think the wheat board must continue. With world marketing conditions as they are to-day, I do not think we dare scuttle the board. I hope the bill will come down in good time so that we may have an opportunity to discuss it in detail. Possibly we can put forward some suggestions which will help the minister in making this whole matter worth while.

speechtext:
The resolution before the house moved by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) reads:
That in the opinion of this house, this parliament should immediately take such steps as are necessary to insure the farmers of Canada a fixed price of ninety-five cents per bushel for number one northern wheat at their local elevator.
Someone has said the fact that this applies only to No. 1 northern wheat confines the effect of the resolution to western Canada, and probably that is correct because it is only in western Canada that we grow No. 1 northern wheat. I therefore wish to take a few moments to discuss with hon. members the suggestion that a fixed price of ninety-five cents be established for wheat at the local elevators, I assume, in western Canada.
A ninety-five cent price at the local elevator would be about the same as $1.15 at Fort William; that is, it would be approximately thirty-five cents higher than the price which was set for this year. In other words, if there had been a price of $1.15 set for the year 1938-39, and the price of wheat had been what it has been, the Dominion of Canada would have found it necessary to put up by way of bonus about $150,000,000. Only to state that amount to the house indicates, I think, that it would be very difficult for any government, no matter what it might call itself, to fix a price of $1.15 for wheat, have the experience tripled which we have had during this last season, and have the system based upon that experience continue for one year longer in the Dominion of Canada.
I tried to state to the house about ten days ago the effect of the set price which we did have in its relationship to the earnings of farmers in western Canada, and I think it was apparent to everyone that even with the eighty cent set price we had created such inequalities in western Canada that very few would advocate a continuance of the pegged
price or set price or fixed price even at the level we had last year. If we were going to assume that the price of wheat would be as low as or lower than that amount for any year in which this ninety-five price was going to be active, it is apparent that no government could retain in existence a price based upon it.

daughters of the farmers of eastern Canada. I want to read to the house to-night a letter I have received from a- farmer; I do not know him at all, but he is a constituent of one of the members of this house from the western part of Canada, and he says that he sent a copy of this letter or a similar letter to the member. This farmer lives at Gladstone, Manitoba. His letter is dated February 17, 1939, and it expresses so well what I think is the opinion of a great many farmers in western Canada that I think it should go on Hansard. It reads:
Hon. J. G. Gardiner,
Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,
As I have just heard on the radio this morning that your department is considering a wheat acreage bonus, I thought I would write and give my views, which are the views of a diversified farmer who has never received any government assistance.
I am not in favour of a pegged price for wheat as it encourages everyone to grow wheat at the expense of oats and barley; also if wheat was at its own level in price, much more of it would be used for feed, also more of it would be held off the market on the farm, thus keeping down the visible supply.
In my own case if prices are low I always hold grain over in portable granaries and when better prices come clear everything pretty well out, and it has worked with me every time.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I would say, without knowing this gentleman at all, that he is probably one of those reasonable men who came from eastern Canada and had considerable experience in farming there before going to the west. His letter continues:
As to an acreage bonus I would suggest it only be on summer fallow. Otherwise there will be a tendency to put land in crop which will never grow a crop owing to weeds, etcetera; also it should not be confined to wheat; otherwise more land will be put in wheat at the expense of oats and barley. Flax being a good price need not have an acreage bonus. I will enclose a copy of this letter to the member for Neepawa.
I remain,
Yours truly,
Alex. Hart.
He apparently was doing some thinking after he had written the letter, because he adds this postcript:
The bonused acreage should be limited.
To my mind that is a man who would be the average farmer in western Canada, a man who is probably thinking of his own business, writing as a result of thinking about it, and not expecting other people in Canada to do unreasonable things in relation to his business.

It has been suggested that the farmer in western Canada needs ninety-five cents a bushel on the average at his own farm in order to maintain him on his farm. I am not going to say anything to-night which would in any way tend to remove that idea from the mind of anyone in this house. I do not think it is necessary to do so. I have here the average price obtained by farmers of western Canada for their wheat, not at Fort William, but at their farms over the last thirty years.
Away back in 1908 that average price was seventy-nine cents; in 1909, eighty-two cents; in 1910, seventy-eight cents; in 1911, sixty-one cents; in 1912, fifty-nine cents; in 1913, sixty-five cents. Those were the years preceding the war, and the average price of the farm during those six years was seventy-one cents.
Then we have the years during the war, 1914 to 1920, in which the price was affected by the war.

speechtext:
It is for the average of his wheat, no matter what the grade. The average price received at the farm in 1914 was $1.24; in 1915, 90 cents; in 1916, $1.29; in 1917, $1.92; in 1918, $2; in 1919, $2.34; in 1920, $1.58. The average price during those seven years was $1.61. These are the average prices for the three western provinces.
If we take the next three years, in which prices were comparatively low, the average price received by the farmer at the farm in 1921 was seventy-eight cents; in 1922, eighty-three cents; in 1923, sixty-five cents; or an average, for those three years, of seventy-five cents a bushel at the farm, or at the farmer's local point.
Again, 1924-1929 was a period of comparatively high prices: 1924, $1.21; 1925, $1.23; 1926, $1.07; 1927, ninety-eight cents; 1928, seventy-eight cents; 1929, $1.03; the average price for those six years being $1.05.
Then, taking the last seven years, which were very difficult years, the returns were: 1930, forty-seven cents; 1931, thirty-seven cents; 1932, thirty-four cents; 1933, forty-seven cents; 1934, sixty cents; 1935, sixty cents; 1936, eighty-eight cents; or an average during the seven years of fifty-three cents.
Over the whole thirty-one years the average is 94-7 cents a bushel or almost exactly the price which is stated in this resolution as that which the government of Canada ought to pay as an initial price to the farmers of western

Wheat Policy-Mr. Gardiner
Canada. For the twenty-four years apart from the war years the average price was seventy-five cents a bushel.
The farmers of western Canada being reasonable people, and a great many of them having had a long experience in the west-I imagine that the gentleman whose letter I read, if he has reached the age of fifty, has probably been over forty years in the particular area in which he resides-will agree with me when I say this, that through the conduct of their business over that long period of time they have obtained an average of about ninety-five cents a bushel for their wheat. These particular individuals do not expect the government of Canada or anyone else to secure for them an average of ninety-five cents by paying it out of the treasury of Canada. By conducting their own affairs they have secured for their wheat an average, over the thirty year period, of ninety-five cents a bushel. If the arguments advanced by hon. members of the social credit group are sound, and ninety-five cents is an amount which would make it possible for a farmer to operate over a long term of years, those who have conducted their affairs in a way to make that possible have been able to get by, as this gentleman says he has, without any government assistance whatsoever.
I am quite sure there are some hon. members who would say, "Well, then, why assist anyone?" Again, I would say that the reason for giving assistance is the fact that not all the farmers of western Canada have had an opportunity of farming in the west over that period of time; the contrary is true of a substantial percentage. Many of them came there without anything at all. Many of them are sons and daughters of those fine farmers of whom my hon. friend spoke, from the eastern part of Canada, who went to the west at a time when conditions in the east were rather difficult, started on farms in the western part of Canada, have done the best they could, and came into this difficult period we are now passing through, when the going is hard largely because world factors and climatic factors have been unfavourable. They are without sufficient resources to see them through their difficulties and into another period when perhaps they will have similar experiences to those of my old Manitoba friend who has had a much longer time and experience wherein to establish himself. In my opinion the government owes it as a duty to people who have run into these difficulties to set up some system under which they can carry on during the difficult period they are now passing through, and get back into a period where they can put themselves on a
Msounder basis financially than they would be *fable to do if we allowed them to be crowded pjfjoff their land and out of their homes and 'into our towns and villages to add to the lists of those who are receiving relief at the present time. So I say, Mr. Speaker, that what we think should be done in connection with a matter of this kind is to take all the facts into consideration and deal with the situation as we find it.
I do not wish to deal at any considerable length to-night with this matter because, when I made the announcement ten days ago of the intended policy of the government in relation to this question, I was aware of the fact that just two days previously there had been held in Saskatoon a meeting of a committee which had been appointed as a result of the conference which has been referred to many times during this debate. That conference was called by the premier of Manitoba. He invited to it people from different parts of Canada and the United States and had discussions upon questions having to do with the marketing of farm products. We were not in any way associated with the calling of the conference. We sent to it all of our officials who were invited to give of their experience, in order that farmers in western Canada and others in business throughout Canada might benefit from that experience. But we had no active part in that conference, nor did we have anything official from the conference, so far as I am aware, until the fourteenth day of the present month, when we received an intimation from the conference in Saskatoon that they were asking for a set price upon wheat for the year 1939-40 somewhat on the same basis as the price had been set for last year.
We had been giving study to this question throughout last summer, and I had carried on negotiations with a great many people before the conference was called in Winnipeg, and following the time that the conference was held in that city. As a result of these conferences and negotiations we had evolved a policy in connection with the matter of handling wheat and assisting the farmers of the area where the greater part of our spring wheat is grown; and having come to the conclusion that it was not advisable to continue a set-up such as we had last year, which resulted in the conditions I outlined to this house ten days ago, we thought it wise to make that known to the people of Canada, and more particularly to those who were discussing the matter in the western part of Canada. And when we made it known, or about that time, we received from that delegation which was meeting in Saskatoon
Wheat Policy-Mr. Gardiner

an intimation that they desired to meet the government on February 28 to discuss the representations which they had to make in relation to the wheat policy of this government. So we decided to go no further with the matter until after to-morrow, when we expect to meet the delegation which has come to Ottawa representing the Bracken conference which was held in Winnipeg, and the meeting which was held on February 14 in Saskatoon. We shall hear their representations to-morrow, and after we have heard them we shall be in a position to discuss further with hon. members policies which we hope to present to the house.
In conclusion, I should like to say that as a result of the findings of the conference which were published in the city of Saskatoon and were forwarded on that particular day to the government, and as a result of the announcement which I made ten days ago, I have been in receipt of considerable correspondence from different parts of western Canada dealing with this particular question. Even before that conference was held, I had considerable correspondence from western Canada. And to indicate to hon. members from all parts of Canada that western farmers are reasonable, let me say that since the results of paying the bonus during last year have been known to the farmers of western Canada, I cannot at the moment recall receiving from any individual a letter advocating a continuance of the policy we followed last year. There have been people who have suggested changes. There have been many who have said we should continue the wheat board. But in no instance that I can recall at the moment-if there were any they were very few-has anyone said, "Continue the wheat board; pay the initial prices you paid last year, and do nothing more with regard to wheat than you did last year."
As I say, people have suggested that changes be made. They have not all agreed on what the changes ought to be. We have studied carefully all the suggestions made by those who have written in, many coming from organizations from one end of western Canada to the other. We have studied carefully the opinions that have come from the eastern part of Canada as well as from the extreme west. We have studied editorial comment in newspapers throughout Canada. We have studied the policies followed in Australia, Argentina, the United States and other wheat producing countries throughout the world. We have tried from this study to evolve a system of handling wheat from western Canada, and more particularly of dealing with the farmer who produces the wheat, which

would be more suitable to the farmers of Canada than could result from simply transplanting to this country any system which may have been adopted in some other country.
In common with every hon. member, I hope that when the legislation comes down it will create better conditions in Canada-I do not say western Canada, but better conditions in Canada than anything we have had, and that in creating better conditions it will not cause as heavy a charge upon the treasury of Canada as some of the systems under which we have been operating. I suggest, if it meets with the approval of the mover, now that we have had a discussion upon his motion which has lasted all afternoon and part of the evening, that it might serve the purpose if he withdrew his resolution. The discussion could be resumed on the legislation when it is brought down. I suggest also that the discussion could be carried on in connection with the third resolution that is on the order paper, still further on the resolution of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), and still further in connection with the resolution of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley). So there will be four further opportunities of discussing the matter, without taking a vote on this resolution now. Therefore, if the hon. member has no objection, I suggest that a withdrawal of this resolution now would serve his purpose.

speakeroldname: Mr. HARRY LEADER (Portage la Prairie) moved:
maintopic: MONTREAL CONSTRUCTION, SUPPLY AND EQUIPMENT COMPANY
subtopic: LIVE STOCK
subsubtopic: PROPOSED APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO ALL PHASES OF THE INDUSTRY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, a special committee of its members should be appointed forthwith to inquire into the conditions pertaining to the Canadian live stock industry in all its phases, and with special reference to the production, sale and distribution of all live stock and live stock products, both in Canada and abroad.
He said: In moving this resolution I am conscious of the fact that I am discussing a subject which is of the greatest importance to the Canadian people. It was said this afternoon that the motion preceding this was of the utmost importance. I believe that to be true, and I believe that the question of live stock is of just as great importance. The two subjects are allied in any system of

Live Stock-Mr. Leader
permanent agriculture. It has often been said that agriculture is the basic industry of Canada. That statement is absolutely true. I think a fair estimate would be that half the people of Canada are employed directly in agriculture, while other thousands are engaged in the transportation, distribution and marketing of agricultural products. And the rest of the population are directly concerned, because it is agriculture that furnishes the food supply for the nation.
The resolution is drafted in broad terms. My idea in so drafting was, that this subject could be discussed from every angle, that we should not be called to order if it was within my power to avoid it. It will be observed that I ask that this special committee be appointed forthwith. That, of course, is now impossible. Some six or seven weeks of the session have passed, and it is not likely that if a committee were now appointed it would be able to proceed as I desired when I sent in my resolution.
The next point in the resolution is that the industry be inquired into in all its phases. The last phrase, which I think takes in almost everything, is "both in Canada and abroad." I hope that other hon. members will join in this debate and present their point of view concerning associated lines of agriculture. For myself I have specialized in the breeding of pure bred stock, so I shall confine my remarks mostly to that phase of the resolution.
I am quite aware of the fact that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is working energetically to evolve some marketing plan or plans that will help the agricultural producers of this country. But it seems to me that we can offer some suggestions that may be helpful to the minister and the officials in his department.
Canadian agriculture is disorganized. The industry lacks direction. Instead of cooperation among the farmers they are engaged in cutthroat competition. That, I think, has been true through all the years that we can remember. As a class we are individualists. While we say we believe in cooperation, I am sorry to have to confess that our farmers have not supported cooperative movements as they should. There is no regulation of production; there is first a scarcity and then a surplus. Witness our past operations in regard to wheat marketing.
To-day that great branch of agriculture to which we refer as the dairy industry is in difficulties. They have a surplus which is bearing down the price of their products. I believe the figures in connection with this industry show that they produced $260,000,000
worth of products last year. I am not going into that phase of the matter to-night, but I get letters from many dairy farmers, complaining bitterly that they have to sell butter fat at a lower price than they should have to sell it at, even when the grass is green and it costs them nothing to feed their cows. It seems to me that the Minister of Agriculture might well say, we must get rid of this surplus of, say 5,000,000 pounds-which after all is really only a week's supply for the people of Canada. I would suggest that if it cannot be sold, it might be handed out for relief purposes, because I believe there are thousands of people on relief in this country, as well as thousands who are not getting relief, who could eat this 5,000,000 pounds of butter and this would provide for them a more wholesome diet.
Then we have the fluctuations in price. I am going to direct the attention of the house to the situation which developed last summer when, within the space of three or four days, the price of hogs dropped 3i cents a pound. This is what agriculturists in every branch of the industry have been up against, and these fluctuations were really what prompted me to ask for this investigation. There is a real demand for an investigation of this kind. There is dissatisfaction everywhere. All hon. members need to do is go to their desks, turn up their files and read the letters the agriculturists are sending to them every day. During the dying days of last session I made the suggestion that a parliamentary investigation be held into the industry of agriculture. About a week or ten days later I received the following letter;
We noted with satisfaction your comments in the House of Commons in regard to a thorough investigation of the live stock situation in Canada. Our board of directors-
That is, the United Farmers.
-discussed this at our meeting yesterday and we are particularly anxious that any investigations undertaken should be conducted by a special committee of the house or other body competent to handle such an investigation. I may say that those of you in the house who are working for such an investigation can be sure of backing from farm organizations engaged in the live stock business and from a great many others as well which are linked together in the Canadian chamber of agriculture.
That is signed by H. H. Haanam, who, I believe, was secretary at that time. Then we find that last year the Manitoba legislature, being concerned as to the state of agriculture, appointed a special committee to investigate the industry. My information is that they did not get very far, because they found this was a matter which really belonged to the parliament of Canada. I believe the minister
Live Stock-Mr. Leader

of agriculture for Manitoba asked that the ministers of agriculture of the three prairie provinces get together in connection with this matter, and I understand this meeting was held in Regina and attended by our federal minister. I am not at liberty to convey the results of that meeting, nor have I the exact information, but this just goes to show that there is deep concern and more or less confusion in regard to the marketing of agricultural products in Canada.
As I pointed out in my opening remarks I intend to deal almost exclusively with the question of live stock. More live stock in Canada would create more labour; there is no doubt about that. In my own experience we employ more men in the winter than in the summer, for the reason that to a large extent' we centre our operations on live stock. I can also state from experience that live stock will compel farmers to sow clover -and crops of that kind, and I know this is perhaps the greatest guarantee against soil drifting, which is quite prevalent in the west. I remember that my land drifted before I got into the Jive stock business, sowing clover and other grass crops, and putting manure on the land. I solved the problem of soil drifting to my entire satisfaction, and I say this method will solve the difficulty. We know also that it will preserve the fertility of the land.
I am amazed when I read of the production per acre in the old land and other European countries, where they have been cultivating the same land for a thousand years or more. They grow perhaps twice as much per acre as we do in western Canada, because they have a permanent system of agriculture, which means they have developed their five stock industry. If we went into live stock to a greater extent, it would, in a measure, solve the problem of our wheat surplus, because more acres would be put into grass and other forage crops, thus taking that acreage out of the production of wheat.
Live stock production is a matter of paramount importance. Someone may ask if Canada is a cattle country. Well, we can produce in Canada cattle as good as can be produced anywhere in the world, and we have demonstrated that over and over again. I remember last year talking to a member of parliament who said our trouble was that we did not have the proper beef here in Canada, and I think he doubted if we could produce it. I just want to remind him of the reception given our cattle when they were placed on the British market in the fresh beef state this year, they outsold even the home product. Yes, we can produce the right kind of cattle in Canada. We have some handicaps, but we

also have some great advantages. I think one of our greatest assets is our climate, which helps produce feeder stock which, when removed to other feeding grounds such as the United States or the old country, make rapid gains. Many times I have read the statement by old country feeders that Canadian cattle were the healthiest and best doers in the world.
Someone may ask if we have markets available. I would say that we have three important markets to which Canadian live stock raisers have access and in which they enjoy advantages shared by live stock raisers in only one or two other countries. First I will deal with the domestic market, which after all, I believe to be of first importance. In reading the Ottawa papers I notice that on the market here one can buy hindquarters of beef for eight cents a pound. I wonder what kind of beef that is. We are selling our best beef in Winnipeg for as much as eight cents a pound live weight; yet those carcasses can be purchased on the market here for eight cents a pound, dressed. I wonder if one could really call it beef. Perhaps a better name for it would be cat meat, which is the term used in referring to dairy cattle. I am not blaming the farmers; I am not blaming the people who buy this meat.
I am just pointing out that consumers will not make an exclusive diet of that sort of food, but will buy just as little as they can get away with. I would take those dairy cows and inferior beef animals and make canner meat of them. I have not the figures before me, but I believe we import thousands of pounds of canned meat annually from South America. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture could find some way of canning those old dairy cows and selling them in place of the meat we import from the Argentine.
I should like to say something about the British market. There we have a preferred position in regard to both live cattle and beef. We are also in a preferred position in regard to live cattle going into the United States. But I am sorry we are not in a more preferred position in regard to sending dressed beef to the United States, that six cents a pound duty is almost prohibitive. I shall . refer to markets later on in my speech.
May I now deal with the proper type that Canadian farmers should be producing. We have three main beef breeds in Canada, and I am going to take the old reliable shorthorns first. I believe they may be classed as the universal breed, because they have gone into nearly every corner of the civilized world. The Scottish shorthorns, which are the pure beef type, are a model of beef. No one who

Live Stock-Mr. Leader
loves beef cattle can find any fault with a model of Scottish shorthorn. Developed in Great Britain and imported to America they made rapid strides. But I believe the Argentine furnishes us with the greatest example in regard to what a good breed of cattle can do. I am sorry I never have had the opportunity, as I know some hon. members have, to view the carcasses as they are hung up in the Smithfield market, and those people declare that the carcasses do not vary an inch in length. They are as uniform as beef carcasses can possibly be.
But there is another breed of shorthorn cattle. This breed also was developed in England, and I believe they are good cattle. But they are not a good beef type. I am sorry to know that many farmers in Canada are trying to get the proper type of beef animal from a dual purpose shorthorn cow. If it is crossed with a good beef bull, there is no doubt it is possible to get a fair animal, but one cannot get the right type of beef which can be expected to compete with the type produced in some other countries.
I wonder how many members in the house to-night have visited the royal winter fair. I assume many have. But I would ask those who have not to take time off next year, so as to visit that exhibition. I would ask them to watch the judging of the shorthorn cattle, and the dual purpose shorthorns, and study the difference between the two breeds. In that way they will get the idea I am trying to convey. It is impossible to get the proper type of beef animal from dairy shorthorns.
The second breed I would mention are the Herefords. or the white-faces. A man who understands the beef business knows that the Hereford is supreme on the ranges of this country. They have made a valuable contribution on this North American continent. I believe it is a well known fact that our best beef comes from the western ranges. I read that the baby beeves which were killed and fetched the top prices in Great Britain-more, indeed, than the Scottish beasts-were baby beeves of the Hereford breed.
I must now turn to my own special breed of cattle, the Aberdeen-Angus. I will not say they are any better than any other breed, but I prefer them, and that is why I am breeding them. Modesty will not permit me to extol the virtues of this particular breed, and for that reason I shall offer to the house some comments from authorities on live stock. I shall quote a sentence from Alvin Sanders, who used to be editor of the Breeders' Gazette, a publication printed in Chicago, and at one time the greatest live stock journal on the North American continent. I noticed this
observation in the Iowa Journal two or three years ago, and I have been saving it, never expecting to use it other than for my own information. The quotation is as follows:
Generally speaking I would say that of all the beef breeds the Aberdeen-Angus is the most highly specialized. It seems most perfectly adapted to the production of superlative block results under high pressure fattening rations.
May I now quote another first class authority, the Hon. Duncan Marshall. This observation, too, was reported in the Iowa Journal and reproduced in the pages of the Farmers' Advocate, an Ontario publication. The Hon. Duncan Marshall, it may be noted, is a past president of the shorthorn association, and when visiting the Smithfield show he said:
When I got to the good steers it was a rare treat. The cross cattle were very fine, and this means the Aberdeen-Angus cross. This was particularly true of the good steers, as with the exception of a few blue ones practically all the high class steers in the show yard had black skins. The results of fat stock shows in various parts of the world must have made it apparent to everyone that cross-bred commercial cattle are continually coming to the front. This is particularly true where the cross has been the blending of Aberdeen-Angus and shorthorn character.
May I quote this further article from our own Commercial Intelligence Journal of February 20, 1937. This will be of interest to hon. members, and of interest to people throughout the country-if they should have an opportunity to read my remarks. The Commercial Intelligence Journal makes this statement.
Buyers have expressed pleasure at the steady improvement in the type and class of cattle shipped from Canada, and particularly in 1936 there has been a much more satisfactory proportion of young cattle, including a large number of well-bred cross-Angus types, which are particularly favoured in Scotland.
In connection with prices, it must be pointed out that the choicest beef cattle received from Canada-young cross-Angus types weighing from 1,000 to 1,150 pounds-have fetched as much as 45s. per live cwt., and that the average for a complete shipment is very much reduced by prices realized for rough, inferior cattle.
I could continue, but that will be sufficient for my purpose. Hon. members may be wondering what connection all this may have with the production of a proper beef type of Canadian cattle, the type which we may hope to export to Great Britain. It is a fact that most of the female stock in Canada, most of the cows, are of shorthorn foundation. That is true in regard to Ireland also. Ireland is using the very finest types of purely beef bred shorthorns, Herefords and Aberdeen-Angus on the shorthorn cows to produce the desired product for Great Britain. That is the point I wish to make.
Live Stock-Mr. Leader

So far, however, as Canadian cattle are concerned, speaking generally their quality is not high. I would not wish to leave the impression that we have not very many fine
herds of all breeds of cattle. But the average cow from which most of these store cattle are being produced is not high. There is no gainsaying that statement, and as proof of it may I point out that I have examined the figures for the last number of years covering shipments made to our stock-yards, and I have found that only one-third of the cattle going into Canadian stock-yards are of the two top grades, namely choice and good, and two-thirds are in the lower brackets, namely medium and common. This statement should convince anyone that the quality of our cattle needs grading up. We must find some way of improving our beef cattle, and there is no easier, quicker or more efficient way of doing so than through the use of better sires.
I am going to say something about the bull policies now in force in Canada. I contend that our policies have been rather slipshod and haphazard. There has been no settled policy, either federal or provincial. Sometimes one province was in and sometimes the other was out. At other times there has been overlapping. Canada has no really stable live stock policy. I was going to give the details of the federal bull policy in Canada, but I see my time is slipping by. Suffice it to say that our policies are certainly not to be commended. I believe the desire is to do the best that can be done, but we must evolve some other method of improving our stock.
I should like to give figures relative to bulls on loan by the federal government, according to the information secured last year from the department. These figures are not divided into dual purpose and beef type animals, so I do not know the percentages. There were 1,342 shorthorn bulls on loan, or seventy-three per cent of the total. There were 357 Here-fords, or nineteen per cent. There were 148 Aberdeen-Angus, or eight per cent. I also obtained the figures with regard to the prairie farm rehabilitation association. They have purchased fifteen shorthorns, three Herefords and two Aberdeen-Angus.
In comparison with what Canada has done in this regard, I should like to refer to the efforts made by Ireland. We must remember that Ireland is our chief competitor. Last year I took it upon myself to send to the old country to get all the information possible in regard to the policies adopted in Great Britain and Ireland. There is certainly a wealth of material available. I shall not give it in

detail, but I have a few notes in regard to the cattle industry in Ireland.
The cattle industry of Ireland is of a twofold character. The cattle are bred for both dairy and beef purposes. The annual value of the dairy industry is approximately $40,000,000, while the value of the beef trade is approximately $100,000,000. Ireland exports approximately 750,000 live cattle to Great Britain annually. The breeding cows are ninety per cent dual purpose shorthorns, and the endeavour is to mate these to high-class beef type bulls, mostly of the shorthorn, Hereford and Aberdeen-Angus breeds. As the Irish farmer cannot afford to neglect the dairy end of his business and must replenish his dairy herd from time to time, a good percentage of dairy shorthorn bulls are used. At the same time they realize that if their store and beef cattle are to find favour in the British market, they must show a measure of superior beef type. The Irish have always taken a keen interest in .their cattle industry, as they realize the importance that industry plays in their national economy.
Down through the years state assistance has been given, mostly in the form of subsidizing the sire. While the various schemes resulted in general improvement, the efforts were voluntary and there were always some who were careless in their breeding operations. This inferior stock found its way to market and hurt the reputation of the Irish cattle. In 1924 a more determined effort was made to improve the qualities of their store cattle. The minister of agriculture introduced a bill which called for the licensing of all bulls in the country, and the act came into force the following year. It is to be noted that this policy of improvement coincided with the lifting of the embargo against Canadian cattle entering Great Britain. They felt sure that we would take advantage of our opportunities, and they were determined to improve the quality of their own stock.
I have dealt with the class of bulls on loan by the dominion government, and I should now like to give the comparative figures for Ireland. I am going to do this by quoting the figures obtained from bull sales which have been held in Ireland. I hold in my hand tables giving the results over a ten year period of the bull sales in Dublin and Belfast, the largest markets in the north and south of Ireland. It would save considerable time if I could have these tables placed on Hansard. First, I would summarize the figures by stating that in the Dublin sales there was a total of 1,540 beef shorthorns sold, the average price received being $178. There were 2,659 Aberdeen-Angus sold, the average price being

Live Stock-Mr. Leader
$205. There were 1,929 Herefords sold, the average price being $212.50. In the Belfast sales, there were 2,012 beef shorthorns sold at an average price of $154.50. There were 985 Aberdeen-Angus sold, at an average price of $163. There were no Hereford sold.

are practically ignorant of the fact that we have a bull scheme in operation. Such schemes are well advertised in Ireland. I have a statement here which I shall not take time to read, but there is no doubt that the quality of the Irish cattle which have been shipped during the last ten years has improved wonderfully, So much for cattle improvement.
I should now like to go back to the markets I mentioned a moment ago. I made the statement that Ireland exported annually to Great Britain approximately 750,000 head of store cattle, and I believe that last year it was in the neighbourhood of 850,000 head. Canada exported on the average in the last five years a little over 27,000 head. This means, Mr. Speaker, that for every one store beast that we sold to the old country, Ireland sold twenty-eight.
I want to say a word about the irregularity of our cattle shipments to the old country, which I believe is one of the main reasons why we have not been able to gain more headway in that market. We have not been able to assure the buyers in Great Britain of a continuity of supply. I made the statement in the house on a former occasion that we should be prepared, if necessary, to bonus our cattle going to Great Britain to provide a certain minimum consignment every month, thus assuring that market of a continuity of supply. I have before me figures of our cattle shipments covering a ten year period, and they go from none in 1929 to 27,307 head in 1938; in one year it was 53,852 head and the next year 6,704 head, which indicates how irregular our shipments to the old country have been. The same applies to our shipment of cattle to the United States. In 1929 we shipped 160.103 head; in 1930, 19,483 head; in 1931, 9,000 head; in 1935, 102,000; in 1937, 208,000; in 1938, 98,408.
We have heard something about filling our quota of cattle going into the United States, and I have figures here for the last three years since we negotiated our first treaty with the United States. In 1936 Canada sent 134,610 head of cattle to the United States, or 86-4 per cent of the quota, while Mexico shipped 21,189, or 13-6 per cent of the quota; in 1937 Canada shipped 131,193 head, or 84-2 per cent of the quota, and Mexico 24,606 head, or 15-8 per cent of the quota; in 1938 we shipped 75,529 head, or 60-3 per cent of the quota, and Mexico shipped 49,741, or 39-7 per cent of the quota. Neither country was able to fill the entire quota last year; but if we had been in a position to take advantage of the United States market, if we had had a sufficient number of cattle, we would perhaps have had about the same

percentage of quota as we had in the two previous years, which averaged eighty-five per cent. I do not intend to follow that any further this evening because it would take too much time.
I want to say something about the possibilities of placing fresh killed beef in the old country. I have a table here showing a total of 11,184,928 long hundredweights of beef imported into Great Britain in 1938. That represents 2,236,985 head of cattle, and of this vast trade Canada's share was 5,200 hundredweight, or 1,300 head-1,300 head in a total of 2,236,985 head! As to the possibilities of placing our fresh killed beef on the British market, first I want to give full credit to the Minister of Agriculture and his department for the experiment they have carried on in the past year, although in my opinion it was not necessary because the feasibility of placing our fresh killed beef on the British market had been demonstrated on three previous occasions. Nevertheless I am here to pay this tribute, that the department has proved beyond any doubt the feasibility of this undertaking, which, after all, is perhaps a very good thing.
We have had various reports in regard to our fresh killed beef placed on the British market and how it was received. One man said it was sensational. '

Mr. Shaw, director of marketing service of the Department of Agriculture, Ottawa, speaking at the conference in Winnipeg, said:
Among the difficulties being encountered are an extremely limited supply of beef of the proper kind.
Does it not mean something to the farmers of this country that we cannot find twenty-five good cattle a week to ship to the old land? It should mean something and it does. I want to suggest to the minister to-night that he place a buyer at the boys' and girls' shows held annually in all parts of Canada and pay a fair price for these cattle in competition with the different abattoirs. I know that the buyers from the abattoirs are good patrons of these sales and that they pay a fair price, but I am going to ask the department to place a buyer there in competition,

Live Stock-Mr. Leader
which may help sell these cattle and will encourage our young boys and girls to raise more beef. There is no doubt they will find the proper type of beef cattle at these shows.
Mr. Shaw goes on to enumerate other difficulties encountered:
Insufficient depth to railway refrigerator cars to allow for hanging full sides, this necessitating the removal of the chuck on the majority of the carcases; lack of necessary facilities at the docks for the safe and economical handling of fresh commodities; insufficient depth in ship's refrigerator chamber to allow hanging of full sides.
All these are serious handicaps. Last year I stated that I believed these cattle should be killed at the seaboard and then loaded directly into our ships and transported, and that there should be no rail haul for dressed beef. If we develop a system in this country whereby we are going to kill these cattle at Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton and elsewhere, it is going to mean railway transportation and the providing of refrigeration facilities, and the producers of this country will have to pay for that equipment. There is no doubt that it will come out of the price to the producers.
Mr. Shaw mentions that dock and shipping facilities are lacking. But we must have these facilities in any event. If we are going to spend money in providing proper equipment, all well and good, but I would hesitate to develop this industry on the basis of having the cattle killed in the interior.and shipped to the seaboard.
I want to quote what the minister said last year when this matter was under discussion. He told us that the beef slaughtered at Birkenhead sold for prices which compared favourably with the prices paid for the best Scottish beef; also that the beef which was killed in Montreal sold at a little lower price; and that which was killed in Saskatoon brought a lower price still. The minister also told us that our Canadian railways did not have proper cars to transport the beef. Again he said that we are carrying on the experiment under the most difficult conditions one can possibly prescribe, and if we can succeed under those conditions we could succeed much better if we had better facilities. There is no doubt that the experiment has succeeded; but I still maintain that if we are going to develop this great industry, our cattle must be killed at the seaboard, placed directly in refrigerator ships, and put on the market in the best possible condition. And so I maintain that our natural advantages should not be lost by the adoption of false methods. The benefits of this industry should go primarily to the producer rather than to the transportation companies and the private packing plants.
I would recommend to the minister that he develop cooperative producers' packing plants. These, I believe, should be followed up by cooperative retail butcher shops for the sale of our cattle in Great Britain.
I would recommend that the federal government discontinue their bull loaning policy. Let them get out of the business altogether and enable the provinces to develop a policy of their own. This is too big a country to develop and provide for these matters from Ottawa; it should be a provincial responsibility, and I believe the provinces would undertake it if they were encouraged to do so. I suggest to the provinces that they carry out policies similar to the ones now in vogue in Ireland. This would leave the federal government with plenty to do. In my opinion they should assist the provinces on a fifty-fifty basis, giving them sufficient financial aid and allowing them supervision of the bull schemes. According to the figures for 1937, the federal government bull policy cost S71,920.52, which is a beginning of the financial assistance they might give to the provinces. The federal government would still guard the health of our cattle.
Another thing I think the federal authorities might do is to discourage the increasing practice of shipping direct to packing plants; they should encourage shipments to the stockyards. We have listened with a great deal of interest to what has been said by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader).
This resolution is very broad in its scope. It suggests that a special committee of hon. members be appointed "to inquire into the conditions pertaining to the Canadian live stock industry in all its phases, and with special reference to the production, sale and distribution of all live stock and live stock products, both in Canada and abroad." The hon. member has covered the subject very well. As he is a breeder of Aberdeen-Angus cattle and I am a breeder of shorthorns, we have something in common. We feel that the farming community of Canada is a basic community. As the hon. member said, agriculture is a basic industry; with that we all agree.
This afternoon we listened to many speeches, all of them dealing with agriculture. Some speeches advocated the fixing of a just price for products such as wheat, oats, barley and rye. For myself, I would just as soon see a just price for live stock, irrespective of whether they are from dairy herds or live stock as sold to the packing plants.
It was my privilege this last summer to go to England and France and see something of the live stock industry in those two great countries, as well as to get some information about the marketing methods practised there. I myself was born on a farm in England, and I know something of the shorthorn cattle industry from the ground upward, particularly its great development in the north of England and the south of Scotland. As the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has said, the cross between shorthorns and Aberdeen-Angus gives the best beef on the Smith-field market.
It is along the line of quality that I would address my remarks this evening, although I intend to speak briefly. I do not know that much was said this afternoon about quality- not as much as should have been said. Hon. members were saying that the price of wheat should be ninety-five cents for No. 1 northern; but most western farmers do not raise No. 1

northern, and the fact is that the great spread in prices, rather than the actual figure for No. 1 northern wheat, is what cripples the farmers in western Canada. The same principle is true of our cattle industry. Many of our finest cattle are sold to the packing plants without much real grading, that is, such as would give the farmer the benefit of the grade. As has been suggested with regard to wheat, so with cattle, we do not always get the benefit of the grade.
As regards the sale of quality cattle, it is vitally important that the government see to it that farmers who raise good cattle get a proper price. The same applies also to the hog industry. Farmers who raise good hogs should reap the benefit of their skill. We know we have a quota from Great Britain for hogs, and that quota is not filled. Year in and year out many thousands more hogs could be shipped to the British market. When I was in England I noticed that on many of the street-cars and buses was the sign, "Eat Danish bacon-it's best." On other buses one would see, "Bacon is best when it's Danish." Wherever you went you would see those signs. We did not see many Canadian signs, although I noticed on the back of the Commercial Intelligence Journal some window-dressing,-"Buy Canadian eggs." Such things are good in their way. But I found that in England they know very little about some of the very best products which Canada raises. [DOT]
I remember that last year the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) suggested that cheese had not been properly advertised in Great Britain before he investigated the matter, and that upon investigation and a proper advertising campaign being put on, a great improvement in the cheese business developed. There is no doubt that it pays to advertise. I suppose that many hon. members receive these communications from different advertising companies stating that if we advertised more, even in Canada, we could sell tremendous quantities of cheese, butter and other products. There is no doubt that if much of the foolishness over the radio were changed into advertising, to tell the people that we have millions of pounds of good butter ready for distribution and sale to Canadian citizens, much more butter would be used. So we are missing even our own market. The dairy producers find a glut of butter on the market and are anxious that it be removed so that they can get a reasonable or just price for their butter.
As other hon. members have said, agriculture is the basic industry of Canada. But

Live Stock-Mr. Coldwell
the foundation of agriculture is the soil. The Minister of Agriculture has a great rehabilitation program for western Canada, and I do not doubt that it is needed in eastern Canada also. We should not be provincial in these matters; we are just as vitally interested in the work of French-Canadian farmers in Quebec or the farmers in the maritime provinces or in Ontario as we are in the western farmers; all farmers should benefit. If the soil is depleted, productive capacity will be curtailed. So the problem of rehabilitation is fundamental.
I have a clipping from the London Daily Telegraph and Morning Post's financial and industrial review of February 13, 1939, in which Viscount Lymington is quoted as saying that one of the greatest wastes in Australia and in Canada is the development of desert areas caused by the destruction of the sod on large sections of land. If the cattle industry were restored to its proper prominence in Canada and proper rotations introduced on cultivated land, this waste would be stopped. Our capital depends upon soil fertility more than on any other factor. If the fertility of the soil is destroyed, our cheap food of to-day will be dear to-morrow. At present we hear about a surplus of foodstuffs, but many economists believe that we are heading for a time when there will not be any too much for the world's needs. Today farmers are in trouble for lack of markets, and in the virgin areas little attention has been paid to conserving the fertility of the land. We have had a great number of "soil miners."

speechtext:
They are gold diggers
on the surface. They are using up the best of the soil and our capital is being lost. Whatever the base of our money, it is ultimately based on the productive capacity, the real value 'of our great dominion. Yet we are actually making deserts, and that is the greatest waste in Canada to-day. So, when talking about live stock production or any agricultural production, we must remember that it depends upon soil fertility, and not waste that fertility, which is our country's capital. Another great waste is the wasted organic matter. One need not go far in western Canada in the fall, after the threshing season is over, to see a lurid glow on the horizon from the burning straw piles. Much of that vegetable matter should be returned to the soil. We have many agricultural experts in the Department of Agriculture who could probably give ideas of more value than my rambling 71492-87
remarks. But what we want is results; we want the experts to see that this waste is stopped.
The hon. member for Portage la Prairie spoke of marketing. I was going to read a statement about marketing by Viscount Lymington. He said:
The profit and costs taken by the distributor mean that so much less food is consumed than should be consumed, that prices are forced down still more owing to what is wrongly called "the world surplus of production."
The idea briefly is that the extent of the spread in prices between what the farmer gets and what the consumer has to pay actually lessens consumption. We know that if one orders a beefsteak in the dining car on the train, one has to pay as much for it as the farmer gets for two bushels of wheat. Consequently this great spread in prices is probably the greatest waste we have in the distribution process in Canada to-day. The removal of that waste should improve our agricultural well-being, raise the standard of living in Canada and benefit our farming industry.
Whatever type of animal we are raising, the first thing to be stressed is quality. Then we must have a comprehensive marketing plan both in Canada and abroad. Both eastern and western Canada will benefit by such a marketing scheme. I do not know whether the hon. member for Portage la Prairie meant that we should give the provinces more control of our cattle and hog raising industries, but we should see that the very best products possible are produced. Then, with our advertising campaign, we should be able to compete with the products of Ireland or Denmark on the British market, and instead of the British people thinking that the best bacon is Danish they will know that the best bacon is Canadian.

speechtext:
This resolution of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) has the support of this group. We believe that a committee such as suggested by this resolution would serve a useful purpose. The resolution is broad and general; it relates to "the Canadian live stock industry in all its phases, and with special reference to the production"-that I think was well covered by the mover-and the "sale and distribution of all live stock and live stock products."
Throughout the country there is a great deal of dissatisfaction regarding the sale and distribution of live stock and live stock products. The spread between what the producer receives and what the consumer pays cannot be understood by either the producer or the consumer. To-day we have two packing firms

Live Stock-Mr. Coldwell

which together control some eighty-five per cent of the entire packing business of Canada. I know they deny that and say it is an overstatement; that if we took into account all the animals slaughtered in local abattoirs and slaughterhouses, that percentage would be greatly reduced; in fact they say it would be cut about in half. But I just draw this to the attention of the house, that after all the price is set, not by the animals slaughtered in local slaughterhouses, but by the animals marketed on the big markets where the packers, because of lack of competition, are practically able to set the price. The price spreads committee . made the statement that two companies controlled eighty-five per cent of that business. So it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this house would be well advised to set up a committee to deal with the matter suggested by the mover of the resolution and to carry on from where the price spreads committee left off in that regard.
We have heard from the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hayhurst) something about the marketing of our products in Great Britain. When I was at my old home there several years ago, we had visiting us a gentleman who had been in Canada for thirty years, whom I had known here and who had gone back to live in Scotland. When we had Danish bacon for breakfast I suggested that Canadian bacon was good, but this gentleman remarked that Canadian bacon did not compare with the Danish' product. The next day I bought some Canadian bacon and took it home to my mother, and I remember that we found it to be quite inferior to the bacon they were accustomed to use. There must be some reason for that. I believe in latter years that condition has been improved owing to the fact that, as I am told, our packing firms are following the example of Denmark and shipping the sides to Great Britain, curing them there to a certain extent.
I think this resolution is worthy of the support of all hon. members, and I hope that when the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) speaks, he will agree to the setting up of such a committee. I have risen on behalf of this particular group simply to say that we shall be glad to give the proposal all our support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to say anything on this resolution, but because of its importance I think I must trespass on the goodwill of the house for a few moments to support the proposal of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). I am only sorry that it was not brought in during an earlier session of parliament, because it opens up a broad

field. My hon. friend took something over his allotted time to discuss the subject, but I believe he only touched the fringe of it. There is so much to be said and so much to be considered in connection with this matter that I do not believe any committee could make a thorough review of all the aspects and phases of the live stock industry, including production and marketing, unless it worked practically every day.
I think we all agree that the live stock industry is not in a flourishing condition at the present time. The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hayhurst) said live stock was the backbone of agriculture. So it is. If we are to maintain the fertility of our farms it is important that we keep a certain number of live stock. This is a most important branch of agriculture; I believe it stands fourth in the matter of returns to the farmers. In the nine years from 1930 to 1938 the value of farm animals produced in Canada was $1,046,000,000. If one adds to that the value of the wool produced, amounting to $18,000,000, and of the poultry and eggs produced, amounting to $482,000,000, one has a grand total of $1,547,000,000, only about $10,000,000 less than the value of our wheat production, about which so much is said in this house. So live stock is a very important industry in Canada, and anything that can be done to strengthen its position and put it on a more profitable basis should and, I believe, will have the support of all members of this house.
My hon. friend who introduced the resolution dealt principally with cattle, but that is only one phase of the live stock industry. We have cattle, horses, sheep, swine and poultry, all of which contribute largely to the revenues of our farmers, and each of which is important in itself. We have some 728,000 farmers in this country, and I believe over half of them derive a considerable proportion of their income from live stock. That means we have over 350,000 units producing live stock in Canada. Because we have all these small units it necessarily follows that they must be serviced. The live stock which they produce must be collected, killed, processed and distributed. During the last quarter century the character of these services has greatly changed. As time goes on, a much larger proportion of our live stock is being slaughtered in abattoirs, which involves increased costs in connection with freight, processing and distribution. For some reason or another these services seem to be continually widening the spread between producer and consumer prices, and I believe, if this committee functions, something should be

Live Stock-Mr. Senn
done in the way of making a particular study of this question, because it seems to me that the spread has become rather too wide, so that it is interfering not only with the price the consumer has to pay but also with the return to the farmer.
After all, Mr. Speaker, we export a very small proportion of our live stock production. In 1937 we exported some seventeen per cent of our cattle, twenty-five per cent of our hogs, less than one per cent of our sheep, and 1-9 per cent of our poultry and poultry products. In all, we exported some eleven or twelve per cent of our live stock products, but the unfortunate thing is that it is the export price which largely determines what the farmer will receive for his cattle and other live stock. It seems to me that question should be considered carefully, because this does not appear to be a fair or sound basis upon which to set live stock prices in Canada.
The matter has been mentioned already, but I should like to say something in regard to the way in which our bacon is marketed in Great Britain. Unfortunately it does not command a comparable price with bacon from other countries. I have before me the weekly market report of February 23, giving the comparative prices of bacon in Great Britain, and unfortunately Canada is lowest of all. The price for a long hundredweight of Canadian bacon ranges from eighty-five to ninety-two shillings, while Danish bacon ranges from ninety-one to 100 shillings and English bacon from ninety to 100 shillings. The bacon more nearly in line with Canadian bacon is Baltic bacon, the price of which ranges from eighty-four to ninety-two shillings per hundredweight. Something should be done about this situation. It is most unfortunate that we in Canada, producing so many hogs of extra good quality, should be forced to take the prices we are taking to-day in the market of Great Britain, our chief market for our exportable surplus.
Something has -been said about the price spreads commission. I can remember that before that commission Mr. Stanley McLean, head of Canada Packers, told us that the price which we receive for Canadian bacon in England is the chief determining factor in the price the farmer receives for his hogs. I believe if we were to send over a better quality of bacon, and bacon of more uniform quality, we would help the farmer materially in the price he receives for his hogs.
A good deal has been said about production. I fully agree with the hon. member who introduced the resolution when he says that our beef cattle are not as good as they should be. Of course we have many good
herds, but if an hon. member were to go to the Toronto stock-yards he would find nondescript cattle there for sale. The prices received for these poorer grades of cattle have a tendency to reduce the price of cattle throughout the dominion, because the same thing is true not only at the Toronto stockyards but at Winnipeg and other points.
Something was said by one hon. member about canning our old dairy cows. That might be one solution of the problem, but I believe we could very well afford to establish a fund to take off the markets altogether those old dairy cows and the cheaper trash appearing on the markets. I believe if we did that we would go a long way toward improving the prices the farmer receives for his cattle.
I said at the beginning I did not intend to speak at length, but may I say this one further word: Too often the farmer's products do not flow on to the market in the right proportions. There are certain periods of the year when hogs, particularly, flow to the markets very rapidly. At other times in the year the packers cannot get enough to supply their requirements. Something should be done to control this situation, and I do not believe it will ever be done unless the Department of Agriculture undertakes it. Farmers cannot very well get together in the matter and regulate the flow of their hogs to the market. I have heard it said that there are times, particularly in the spring and fall, when the hogs are coming out so rapidly the abattoirs are unable to handle them, and they are left in pens for three or four days. As a result they fail in flesh; there is considerable shrinkage ; they have to be fed and, naturally, when the abattoir has an over-supply it is not inclined to pay the price it might otherwise pay if some sort of regimentation were carried out, and the farmers could be induced to bring their hogs along more evenly throughout the year.
Something wras said about the law of supply and demand governing our prices. It seems to me there must be some correlation of that law of supply and demand, if it is to govern. In my view that, too, is the duty of our Department of Agriculture. I say that because unless something is done by way of setting up a marketing board, or of setting up some method of cooperative marketing, we are not going to solve the farmers' price problem, which after all is the most serious one with which he is faced.
I have said before, and I now repeat, that if the farmer is given a reasonable price for his product we need not worry about his producing the goods. He will produce them
Live Stock-Mr. Evans

in quantity and quality. As long as he does not get a reasonable price he will be discouraged. The effect at the present time is that he is not producing as he should produce, and is not taking the care he should take.
I believe the resolution is worthy of the support of the house. I repeat that I am sorry it was not brought in at a former session, because if the matter is to be thoroughly investigated by a committee, undoubtedly such investigation could not be completed before the end of the session when it would be too late for the government to take action on any suggestions the committee might make.
