speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say. only a few words with respect to the live stock policy in the debate on the resolution presented to the house by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader). May I say at the outset that he deserves a great deal of credit for presenting in an able manner the difficulties live stock breeders are having in marketing their product, and the trouble they are having in controlling the breeding of good beef cattle. I agree with him to this extent, that we should breed good beef cattle-not to quantity, but to quality. In Saskatchewan in the past two or three years our herds have been reduced. May I say to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) that at the present time in Saskatchewan we have a situation which offers to his department and to the department in Regina an opportunity to supervise the replacement of herds, and particularly the breeding stock, in southern Saskatchewan, so that we may breed a quality of cattle which will meet the demands of the beef market.
In the short time I shall take I should like to direct my remarks more particularly to the live stock industry in Saskatchewan. That portion of the province I have the honour to represent is particularly adapted to the raising and producing of good live stock, including cattle, horses, sheep and hogs.
For the past number of years the ranchers in southwestern Saskatchewan have endeavoured to develop their herds to meet the market demands for first quality beef. In that part of the province I believe we have some of the best herds of white-faced cattle to be found anywhere on the north American continent. I have in mind one particular herd owned by a large rancher. This ranch straddles the border of Saskatchewan and Alberta and consists of about 10,000 or 12,000 head of cattle, and I would say for the last
[Mr. Senn.1
fifteen or twenty years they have been using the best males money could buy, in whitefaced cattle. To-day the herd is possibly as good as any pure bred herd on the north American continent, although they are not registered.
Two years ago from the town of Maple Creek we marketed something like 16,000 head of cattle. About 2,000 of these were marketed under the emergency policy of the federal Department of Agriculture, but the balance were either beef or store cattle which were shipped to eastern Canada. I was particularly interested in one shipment that went to the maritime provinces. The gentleman who bought these cattle came out west in the latter part of 1937 when the store cattle had been nearly all shipped out, and there was nothing left but spade heifers. Many of the feeders in eastern Canada, particularly in that portion of the maritime provinces from which he came, did not know anything about this class of cattle. I went out with him to a rancher who had, in a feeding lot, about 200 head of this particular kind of cattle, and he chose a carload of twenty-eight head, which was shipped to Truro, Nova Scotia. I asked him to keep in touch with me and let me know the success of the shipment. Later on I received word that these cattle had fed out satisfactorily and had been shipped overseas.
When the herds in Saskatchewan were reduced in 1937, there were 508,000 head of all classes of cattle shipped out, and under the federal marketing policy, about 74,000 head. There were a lot of immature and what is commonly known as scrub cattle taken out of the province. Naturally this left the best type of cattle in the hands of the farmers and ranchers. Under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act the federal government has been setting up community pastures in the drought areas, and in 1937 many of these small ranchers and farmers will keep their best cattle in these pastures. As the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) has said, under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act there were purchased twenty pure bred bulls last year to be put in these community pastures for the production of a better class of live stock.
The federal bull loaning policy is in operation in Saskatchewan, and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has already given the number of pure bred sires that have been put out during the years this policy has been in operation. From 1933 to 1938 there have been put out under the federal bull loaning policy in Saskatchewan, 371 shorthorns, 116

Live Stock-Mr. Evans
Herefords, forty Aberdeen-Angus, three red poll and one Holstein. It is interesting to note that under the emergency policy of 1937, the greatest number of scrub and inferior cattle came from those areas where dairying was being carried on. The better class of cattle came from the ranching areas in the southwest which breed particularly white-faced cattle. As the hon. member for Portage la Prairie has stated, this is the best class of beef cattle, together with shorthorns and black-poll Angus.
Then we have in operation in Saskatchewan what is known as the pure bred sire areas act, which came into force in 1927. This act becomes operative on the application by a municipality that the area within that municipality become what is known as a pure bred sire area. The act covers bulls, stallions, boars and rams, and stipulates that the animals used in the particular municipality shall be pure breds and come up to a certain standard. In the case of the hog and sheep families, good sires may be used which are not pure breds. There are sixty-nine municipalities in the province operating under this act, and very good results have been obtained in the ten years it has been in operation. However, there have been set-backs because of the drought.
We also have in that province a.company which will loan a certain amount of money to a farmer with which to buy a good type of female for the production of beef. This company is known as the Dominion Agricultural Credit Association, and it operates in the three prairie provinces. They have inspectors who go out to choose the females for breeding purposes, and also to inspect the farm and ranch where the females are to be kept to see that there is proper water, shelter and feed. Credit is extended to the farmer or rancher for a period of three years, and payments are made from the production of the animal.
We hear a great deal about the exporting of beef, and I should like to refer briefly to this matter. We had some experience in this regard in the southwestern part of the province in 1933 and 1934, and the results were not very satisfactory. I notice from the statistics of the Department of Agriculture that in 1933 we exported to Great Britain a little over 50,000 head of cattle. The exports in 1934 numbered 53,000 head. My experience is that this is not the best way to export our beef. For example, I know of two cars containing fifty-six head which were shipped in 1934. These cattle were of the same breed as those raised by the hon. member for Portage
la Prairie. They were a splendid type of animal weighing about 1,280 pounds. They were billed through from my home town to Montreal, from which point they were to be shipped to Birkenhead, England. When they were inspected at Winnipeg, one steer was taken out because it showed signs of lump-jaw. This animal was sold on October 14 and brought $27.50. The other fifty-five head went through to Birkenhead where they were sold, but the rancher received only $17.50 a head, compared with the $27.50 he received in Winnipeg for the steer showing lump-jaw.
I agree with the hon. member for Haldi-mand (Mr. Senn) and the hon. member for Portage la Prairie when they say that it would be much better to have our steers slaughtered at the sea port and shipped as fresh killed beef. In that way we could distribute our shipments over the year to much better advantage than we can when shipping the live steers. The low prices that the rancher and beef breeder received for their cattle in 1934 resulted in our shipping to the old country in 1935 only 6,704 head of cattle.
I should now like to say a few words on the horse industry. In the portion of the province from which I come, many horses of various types and classes are raised on the ranches. We have a good type of heavy draft horse, but apparently the western horse does not meet the demands of the eastern market to the extent we should like. I think there might be some way of having supervision of the marketing of our western horses.
We also have in southwestern Saskatchewan an association known as the Hunter and Saddle Association, of which we have a breeding station at Shaunavon and another at Maple Creek. The association is given assistance by the federal Department of Agriculture, which supplies a thoroughbred stallion to each breeding station. This service has been in operation for about ten years with satisfactory results. Last year at the Hunter and Saddle show at Shaunavon and Maple Creek some splendid animals were shown, and some of them changed hands to eastern buyers at satisfactory prices. I would commend to the minister that assistance be continued in this type of breeding in Saskatchewan, and I should also like to see some assistance given in a horse marketing policy in the province of Saskatchewan.
I am quite prepared, Mr. Speaker, to support the resolution of my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie, asking for a committee to investigate the marketing and production of live stock.
Live Stock-Miss Macphail

Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce): Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a couple of minutes to say that I support the resolution, largely because of what I think a study by a committee of this house would lead to. I believe, if a group of members studied the live stock problem in all its phases, both domestic and foreign, it would inevitably come to the conclusion that we had to have commodity marketing and a more comprehensive marketing scheme, and the sooner we come to that conclusion the better, not only for the live stock industry but for all farmers. Further, a study would bring to light such facts as would tend at least to lead to the organization of producers. As a matter of fact, they could not take advantage of a marketing scheme until they were organized as commodity groups, though at the rate the government is moving towards marketing they will have plenty of time to organize. But undoubtedly a study would lead to further light on the subject, and the farmers are themselves coming to the conclusion that commodity organization and a comprehensive marketing scheme are necessary.
Then I think a committee would also lead to the conclusion, as the price spreads inquiry did, that we need cooperative or publicly owned processing plants.
A comprehensive study would also bring us to the conclusion that we cannot allow domestic prices to be set by very small surpluses, and in that regard I think we shall have to take a leaf out of the manufacturer's book. He has always sold his surplus abroad at lower prices than he got in the home market. Even though the transportation charges might be very high, his surplus was sold in foreign countries for very much less than at home. I think we are coming close to the time of a two-price agriculture, and anything that will hasten the day of better prices for domestic consumption will be welcomed by our farmers.
Such a study I think would also convince Ontario people and the east generally that the thing that would be most disastrous to eastern farmers would be for western farmers to go into mixed farming in a big way, that when they go into cattle production in a big way it is a sad day for Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes. It would affect Ontario very much, and such a study by the committee might get the idea over to Ontario farmers, including one very prominent one who happens to be premier at the moment. It is time we understand that any change from wheat to general farming in western Canada is going

to involve eastern Canada in an entirely new set of problems added to those they already have. So, while it does look like a pretty large order a special committee could get started at all events, and it may be that if this is not the last session of this parliament, and there are now some signs that this is true, if the committee does not get finished this year, it could continue its labours next year. At any rate the sooner we start, the sooner we get through, and the sooner we may get results.

Mr. Speaker, a year ago the hon.
member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) suggested that a committee be appointed to study the marketing of live stock and the live stock question generally. At that time I suggested to him that a study was being made of the situation existing in relation to live stock production and live stock marketing, and that we hoped during this session of the house to bring down certain legislation. This year the hon. member placed his resolution on the order paper early in the session, and I intimated to him at that time that we had certain legislation under preparation and almost ready for introduction, but suggested to him that it would still be well to have this matter discussed in order that the views of different members might be placed before the government before the legislation was introduced.
I would have no objection, and the government, I am sure, would have none, to a committee of the house being appointed to study this matter, if it is thought advisable to do so; but I should like to suggest that a few days be allowed to pass until that legislation is introduced, and then if it does not meet the situation as members desire to have it met, we can still go on with an investigation by a committee of this house.
There have been some questions raised tonight as to which I should probably say a word or two before eleven o'clock. One of them has to do with the trial shipments rve have made this year to the Smithfield market in Great Britain. As has been stated by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie and others, the type of beef which is being sent over is what is known as baby beef; that is, beef which dresses around 450 pounds. We have been sending over twenty-five head a week.
A year ago it was suggested that this beef be killed at the seaboard, and some of our friends from the eastern provinces, the maritimes particularly, suggested that we might select that beef in the maritime provinces. At that time I think I was able to indicate

Live Stock-Mr. Gardiner
that marketings in the maritime provinces were so small that it would be impossible for us to select the type of beef we required in any of the marketings that are made in the maritime provinces. As a matter of fact, during the summer we had considerable difficulty in selecting, even on the Toronto market, the twenty-five head of the type required by the Smithfield market, and there were, I think, three weeks, in succession, in the middle of the summer-I am speaking from memory- during which we were unable to find, on the Toronto market, the twenty-five head of what are known as baby beef. We had therefore to send over twenty-five head of heavies. Those heavies did not bring us so good a price as the Scottish beef, and they did not compete with the Scottish beef.
The lighter type of animal, fed to market at the younger age, is in great demand on the British market now, as it has been for some years. This is because of the fact that in Britain, as in this country, many of the younger members of the family, when they reach the age of eighteen to twenty, leave home and are not to be found in the home circle. A larger and larger percentage of the homes in British cities, as in Canadian cities, are today occupied by two or three people. Two or three people do not want big cuts of beef. In the old days the habit was to cook large roasts and to have them as cold meat at succeeding meals, but that is not the practice today. With electric heating and cooking and all that kind of thing, the smaller roast is required by a considerable percentage of those who are eating meat in the old country. For that reason they prefer the smaller type of animal, well finished. It is that demand which made it possible to sell twenty-five head of what are known as baby beef on the British market week by week throughout the past year, and to get the very best results and the very best satisfaction from the selling.

I have a great deal of sympathy for the suggestion made by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Miss Mac-phail), but even a marketing set-up based on commodity production would not bring the results that are obtained in Denmark unless we market our products in the same way as they do in Denmark. Their pork and bacon production in that country is absolutely under control of a cooperative. The cooperative owns all the hogs; they allow people to feed them only if they feed them properly; they dictate what they are to be fed, and how much; they determine when they are going to market them, and when they are ready to go to market they kill them in abattoirs which are under their control, load them in boats which are their own, put them in compartments properly fitted up for the shipment of bacon, send them to Great Britain, and keep control of them until they are actually placed on the market. Anyone who knows conditions in Denmark and compares them with conditions in this country knows that it will be a long time before any country as widely spread as the Dominion of Canada, with all the varying conditions we have here, can emulate what is being done in Denmark. Nevertheless we can do a great deal to assist.
Last summer I had the privilege of visiting the home of Andrew Anderson, who is farming at Innisfail, Alberta. If anyone wants to see a real basis for the solution of our hog problem in Canada he should visit that farm. I think Mr. Anderson is a Dane: he is

The Late J. W. Rutherford
either a Dane or a Norwegian; he has been farming there for a considerable time. I dropped in at his place last summer. He was then busy equipping a pig house in which he hoped to have pigs born in every month of the year. He had a heating plant in it, and had it fitted up so that he could have his pigs coming in every month. I said to him, "Does it pay to do that kind of thing?" "Well," he said, "it would not pay me to do anything else," and he said, "probably it would not pay me as much as it does pay me if everybody else in Canada did what I was trained to do before I came to this country, namely, have hogs to sell every month of the year. Having hogs to sell each month, I can make good money feeding at the price at which we can obtain feed in this western country." I think that is the basis for a solution. We can investigate the question from now until doomsday; but if we just place the emphasis on the fact that someone in the packing plant is trying to get an advantage over us, and we do not play our own part in trying to see that the hogs are produced in the proper way and at the right time, we shall never accomplish for agriculture in this country what it is possible for us to accomplish.

Legislation will be brought down; and if that legislation does not meet fully with the approval of hon. members we can give consideration in a very few days' time to the suggestions contained in the resolution.
